en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of National Teacher Shun’o of Suiryō:
I have observed what is recorded in the *Mahābrahmādeva-putra-prcchā-saṃśaya-vinodana-sūtra*:

when Brahmādeva offered a golden *pārijāta* flower to the Buddha and requested him to preach the Dharma, the Buddha held up the flower to show the assembly; among the hundreds of thousands of beings, including devas and humans, none could fathom its meaning.
Only the ascetic Kanakavatsa broke into a smile. The Buddha said, "I have the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the wondrous mind of Nirvana, the true mark which is markless;
I entrust it to Mahākāśyapa. Alas! Is this not the beginning of the *dhyāna-pāramitā*? Human beings are born in stillness;
their nature is fundamentally perfect and luminous, like the great lunar orb whose radiance shines everywhere. All sentient beings...
Within the realm of Mount Meru, all things possessing the nature of moisture—whether vast as rivers and oceans or minute as ponds and pools—without exception possess the moon.
Thus, where there are ten billion bodies of water, there appear ten billion lunar forms. Yet when one looks up and gazes upon them, the moon in the central sky has never been divided.
The moon is a metaphor for the *dharmatā* (intrinsic nature); the water is a metaphor for the objective realm (*viṣaya*). One becomes ten million.

Ten million makes one. From the beginning, there is neither that which responds nor that which does not respond; essence and function share a single source, and the manifest and the subtle are without interval.
The Great Sage’s entire being is wholly true, never losing its nature of perfect luminosity, like the moon in a cold pond.
There is not the slightest obstruction or veil; its pure radiance blazes forth brilliantly.
Yet ordinary beings, driven by habitual tendencies and bound by karmic consciousness, pursue only delusion and darkness. It is like the moon in turbid water: it is already obscured and invisible.

Furthermore, when fierce winds arise from all sides, tossing the waves and surging the billows, and fish and dragons appear and disappear amidst shifting illusions and confusion—how could one hope to find even a single opening?
In this clarity, nothing can be apprehended. Therefore, the mind of the sage is centered on stillness; though it is still, it is not merely still, for even in movement it is still.
The sentiments of ordinary people are enslaved by movement; though they move, they are not still, and even in stillness they are moved.
Our Great Master Daruma came specifically to this eastern land to transform and deliver sentient beings through the mind-study transmitted by Kāśyapa.
He sought to clarify turbidity as emotion and to still the waves into tranquility, entering directly into the stage of awakening before coming to rest.

Thus, his essence is eternally quiescent—a quiescence that is itself non-quiescent; his wisdom is eternally illuminating—an illumination that is itself non-illumination; and his responsiveness is eternally functioning.
Yet it employs the useless. Reaching this state, its subtlety is difficult to name. Nevertheless, it is not easily attained in a single step.
Only through oneness and emptiness does one sit and forget the body. Whether moving slowly or gradually, one dwells forever with the divine spirit (*shenming*).

Fearing that the mind may disperse and fail to reach harmony, one establishes a "doubting mind" (*yi-qing*) to unify it. Fearing that one might stop short upon reaching the goal, one relies upon goodness.
He skillfully guides them by drawing them forth, mindful that they might become biased and lose their correctness; he pulls those submerged in the depths back to safety.
His way was likely just like this. The various masters of successive dynasties each honored what they had heard, maintaining this tradition without daring to let it falter.
It reached our Master Yuwang Hongguo, who rose from the shores of the Eastern Sea, grasping the wheel of the Dharma and widely opening the gates of salvation. Bodhidharma—

The Way of the Great Master has flourished once more with brilliant revival. Those who have entered his gate are none other than dragons and elephants among men, and the Venerable Zhuyuan Dao was renowned as one who had attained the essence of the world.
Now, our Chan Master Shuzhong Yun is a入室 (入室) disciple—meaning a direct successor who has entered the inner chamber—of Zhuyuan.

Initially, he received ordination from the Venerable Yuansou Duan and heard many essential points of the Dharma; now, having prepared incense to repay his debt of gratitude, he has returned to [the lineage of] Zhuyuan.
Master Daogong. Subsequently, in deference to the requests of the multitude, he emerged from seclusion to serve as abbot at Lingyan on Mount Xiangshan and Ruiyan on Mount Huangyan.

Those who took refuge in him increased day by day, and his fame spread throughout the Eastern Barbarians (Japan). Envoys came to present tribute to the Middle Kingdom and concurrently submitted a petition for him to reside there as abbot;
the Master accordingly accepted.
An imperial edict summoned him to the Southern Capital, but he resolutely declined to go.

The Emperor, pitying his advanced age, granted his request. He was about to retire and live in seclusion by the Qín River when his disciple Jūding requested a preface for me regarding two of the Master’s discourses.
Having long heard of the Master’s reputation and having previously had occasion to glimpse his words, I [accepted].
12. Now, having further obtained a complete view of it, I was struck as if by a crashing thunderbolt and driven like a swift whirlwind;
mountains and peaks shifted, the waters of the sea stood still, spirits wept, and demons fled. Upon hearing this, all ordinary sentiments were utterly extinguished.

Therefore, I shall not decline to examine and resolve the doubts recorded in the *Jueyi jing* (Sutra for Resolving Doubts) in order to reveal the source of Chan, and to clarify the nature [of mind] through the metaphors of the Dharma-water and the moon.
Yuan takes the teaching of Bodhidharma as the source of his learning and places it at the head of every scroll. I am old and infirm;

when various requests for writings have come before me, I have declined them all. That I alone now take up this matter for the Master is out of compassion for the decline of the Great Dharma and because I rejoice in the Master’s words being in accord with the Way.
Preface by Song Lian of Jinhua, Academician and Attendant Lecturer at the Hanlin Academy, Grand Master of the Second Grade with Harmonious Compliance,
Compiler of Imperial Edicts, Joint Editor of the National History, and Concurrent Attendant on the Crown Prince, on the twenty-second day of the tenth month in the seventh year of Hongwu.
Preface to Volume One of the Catalogue of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shuzhong.
Recorded Sayings of the Abbot of Lingyan Guangfu Chan Temple on Mount Xiangshan,
Volume Two;
Recorded Sayings of the Abbot of Ruiyan Jingtu Chan Temple in Huangyan.
Volume Three:
Ancient Verses and Minor Buddhist Rituals; Volume Four: Ancient Verses and Minor Buddhist Rituals.
Verses of Praise and Eulogies,
Volume Five:
Verses and Dharma Discourses.
Volume Six:
Regulated Verse, Quatrains, Prefaces and Postscripts,
and Records of Spiritual Practice.
Table of Contents (End).
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shuzhong, Volume One.
Compiled by his disciples, including Zongfu, former abbot of Wanshou Chan Temple in Changguo.
Record of the Sayings at Guangfu Chan Temple on Lingyan Mountain, Xiangshan.
The Gate to the Monastery: A single phrase for entering the gate—how difficult is it to see? Once the mechanism is set in motion, the eastern door opens and the western door closes.
*He!* (A shout).
The Patriarch’s Hall. The chestnut thorn. The diamond circle. Throwing it here and casting it there, from this land to the Western Heaven.
Occupying the chamber—struck once and it is accomplished. Seizing the topknot and heading to the yamen—no need for even a single blow.

Embracing the stolen goods while crying out for injustice—even if one were to hit the mark a hundred times out of a hundred, employing both release and gathering together, none of these would be of any use beneath my Lingyan gate. Pick up the staff.
He drew a line with his staff and said: "The Qian trigram has three unbroken lines;
the Kun trigram has six broken lines. Regarding the Monastery Preface: Before entering the Gate of Lingyan, you all are the hosts and this mountain monk is the guest.
Once you have entered the Gate of Lingyan, this mountain monk is the host and you all are the guests. Now, how do you express the single phrase in which host and guest are merged in harmony?
The iron Kunlun mountains beneath the golden incense burner;
the informal exchanges of the outer circle; the nostrils of the Master; the eyes of Bodhidharma—all are right here. If one discusses their fundamental source:
They arise from the same source; yet when comparing their merits, each possesses eight hundred [qualities]. In between lies some ambiguity that no one, ancient or modern, has ever articulated.
(The *Dushu* says: "The sword that kills, the blade that gives life."
Ascending the seat, he offered incense to pray for the Emperor.
Having finished, he next held up the incense and said: "When the ancients appeared in the world, they offered incense to repay the kindness of their Dharma-mother.

When people of today appear in the world, they offer incense to repay the kindness of the world. I, Venerable Yun, do neither of these. In years past, while traveling on pilgrimage, I arrived at Mount Zituo."
In the midst, meet this old patch-robed monk. He has no dharma to bestow, and I have no dharma to receive.
Simply produce it from within this state where there is neither bestowing nor receiving, and offer it as an offering.

The late Venerable Zhuyuan Dao, who formerly resided at Jianyan Chan Temple in Kunshan, did not seek to repay his virtue or requite his kindness, but simply desired that everyone understand the matter.
He then adjusted his robes and took his seat. Master Zhimen struck the gavel and said:

"In this Dharma assembly, you dragon-like and elephant-like disciples, you should contemplate the primary meaning. The Master then delivered these words: "The primary truth is, right now, Master Zhimen..."
I have already finished splitting the flowers with everyone here. If you could have realized it even before the sound of the mallet was struck, you would still be considered a dull-witted fellow;
how much less worthy of admiration are those who step forward to listen for instructions?

Nevertheless, while the official path does not admit a needle, the private way allows for carriages and horses. Should anyone have doubts, feel free to ask questions. (The dialogue is not recorded. He then said:
The profound purport of Mount Ling, the true mechanism of Shaoshi—its brilliance cannot be matched by the sun and moon;
its vastness cannot be matched by empty space. Majestic and operating alone, it is expansive and impartial. To contemplate it is to err; to deliberate upon it is to go astray.
The five thousand and forty-eight fascicles are like describing food to others; the seventeen hundred "entanglements" are like using a conch shell to measure the ocean. As for the present...

Throughout all quarters, there are none who do not say that [the masters] are driving away their plows and seizing their food, valuing only that the ancestral style (*zongfeng*) not fall into decline.
Little do they realize that this is precisely like giving fire to one suffering from heat or ice to one suffering from cold—it only serves to increase the severity of their ailment.

When Xing Lingyan speaks thus, it is not that he is degrading the worthy to serve as commoners and inviting the laughter of the world; rather, it is like knowing a physician only after one’s arm has been broken three times, or gaining wisdom only after having experienced many people.

To understand this mark: those who are spiritually sharp need not hesitate or deliberate; they should simply enter directly with a single blade, sweep away the calamities of war, and enjoy peace and prosperity—how joyful this would be!
To entertain even a moment’s hesitation is to be ten thousand miles from the white clouds.
Again, it is related: On Mount Tai there was an old woman. Whenever a monk asked, "Which way does one go on the road to Mount Tai?
she would simply say, "Go straight ahead. As soon as the monk had walked a few paces, the woman would say, "What a fine monk, going off like that!"
Zhaozhou said, "I shall go and test this old woman. Zhaozhou questioned her in the same manner, and she answered him in the same manner.

Upon returning, Zhaozhou told the assembly, "The old woman has been tested and exposed by me. The Master [Linji] commented: "The old woman was like wood gnawed by insects, where patterns happen to form by chance.
Zhaozhou saw the 'righteousness' and acted with courage, yet he ended up making a great display of it. Do you all understand?"
Do you understand? When the clouds have gathered and the rain has cleared, the vast sky is wide open; a pair of mandarin ducks cannot be fully captured in a painting.

*Small Assembly:* Lingyan is steep and precipitous; those who reach it find it difficult to do so. Those who have already reached it enjoy peace and security, while those who have not yet reached it remain solitary and exposed.
For those who are solitary and exposed, this is precisely the time to step forward. For those who are enjoying their security, they must further take a step back.
Regarding oneself, it is said: "Matters do not have a single direction. Sometimes the head is turned into the tail; sometimes the tail is turned into the head.

In gathering and releasing, in traversing horizontally and vertically, how could one remain confined by fixed tracks? When Mahākāśyapa shut his room and Vimalakīrti remained silent, though these were called the full manifestation of the orthodox command, they nonetheless had not yet reached the ultimate.
This mountain monk, at the very beginning of entering the gate tonight, as we gather here together—
First: I have established three articles of law for you all. First, you must not give rise to the view of a Buddha. Second, you must not give rise to the view of the Dharma.
Third, you must not say that you do not give rise to the view of a Buddha or the view of the Dharma. If you act in accordance with these, [you shall be saved].
"Take it for granted that his eyebrows will knit together. Suddenly he picked up his staff and said, "A man of clear eyes has no fixed patterns.

Looking down from the highest heights, there is nothing more; leveling out from the lowest depths, there is always enough. He struck the ground with the staff. "The iron ox does not eat the grass by the fence;
he goes straight to sleep atop the summit of Mount Sumeru."
Again, Master Dahui raised this matter and asked a monk, "It is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing.
How do you understand this? The monk said, "I understand. Dahui said, "You have understood the seven generations of ancestors in your house. The monk then gave a shout.
Dahui said, "Just now you said 'I understand,' and now you shout. What does that have to do with 'it is not mind, it is not Buddha, it is not a thing'?"
A monk hesitated to deliberate upon the matter. Dahui immediately struck him. The Master [Zhaozhou] comments: "The Elder Dahuai maintained this one pivotal point;
even if one were to take the great void as a mouth and Mount Sumeru as a tongue, it would still be difficult to fathom the application of its function.
Yet, when examined closely, it cannot be said that he was entirely without gain or loss. At that time, had that monk been a person of true caliber, upon seeing him give..."
When asked thus, he simply said to him: "At the third watch, one passes through the Iron Ring Mountains. Is this not truly leaving the past behind and cutting off the future?
He struck his whisk. A bamboo staff transforms into a dragon; the deluded person bails out the night pond.
The Special Envoy ascends the hall: "The Great Master Bodhidharma came ten thousand *li* from the West, intending to be a man who could convey a letter and deliver a message.

Yet, when he faced King Liang face-to-face, all his effort yielded nothing but the words, 'I do not recognize you. [The Master] picks up the staff: Herein lies guest and host; herein lie ritual and music.
With hands and face clearly distinguished, the full moon is revealed; at the crown of the head, the golden bell is shaken."

Duo ascended the hall and said: "If you understand Chan and understand the Way, you are bound by that understanding. If you do not understand Chan and do not understand the Way, you are bound by that non-understanding.
It is like seeking the tracks of a bird in the sky or looking for the footprints of a fish in the water."

Ascending the hall, he said: "If there is a question, there is an answer—this is like lighting a lamp after the sun has set. If there is no question, there is no answer—this is like cutting off the horns of a rabbit.
To take another path is to go ten thousand *li* to Yuzhou; to directly accept it is to proceed with caution. He held up his staff, drew a line, and said:
"The heavens lean toward the southeast; the earth leans toward the northwest. Linji’s little fellow possesses only one eye. He struck the floor with the staff.
[The Master] leaned on his staff and gave a shout.

He ascended the hall and said: "The bright moon shines upon the high crags; the hanging waters echo over the front ridges. How clear are the ears and eyes! In profound stillness, one realizes the nature of the mind.
Alas, Avalokiteśvara! The snow from the eaves comes to fill the well. He descended from the seat.
Ascending the hall, he held up his whisk and said: "The World-Honored One held up a flower; Bodhidharma faced the wall.

Even down to later times, there were those who administered blows or shouts, or who brandished pitchforks and danced with ritual tablets—manifesting all manner of divine and demonic forms. All of these emerge from right here.
He cast the whisk down and said: "Better that this good thing had never happened at all."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Fish take water as their life; birds take trees as their home. If the trees are cut down, the birds find a place to rest;

if the water is exhausted, the fish preserve their lives. But tell me, since the trees have been cut down and the water exhausted, for what reason do the birds instead find a place to rest and the fish instead preserve their lives? If you can understand it here, I grant that you have a point of entry."
If you could not clarify this matter just now, it might be granted that you have a point of entry. Setting aside for a moment whether one can clarify it or not, consider this:
Zhuang Zhou said, "In the Northern Ocean there is a fish; its name is Kun. It transforms into a bird; its name is Peng.
At that very moment, if you call it Peng, it is still the Kun; if you call it Kun, it is still the Peng. Now then—?
The Kun and the Peng—do they have a distinction, or not? If you say there is a distinction, they originally arose from a single essence.

If you say there is no distinction, they have nevertheless manifested as two forms. Ultimately, how shall one judge this? *Striking the whisk:* "The thread on the tip of the pole is for you to handle;
Without disturbing the clear waves, the meaning is naturally distinct."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The meaning of the Patriarchs contains no separate dharma. When walking downstairs, one’s shoes are worn through; when sleeping on the bed, one’s socks are pulled off.
To act just like this is too much of a riddle; not to act like this leaves nothing to resolve. The water buffalo of Mount Gui; the wild ducks of Baizhang."
"Carrying water and dragging mud is not worth looking at; the halo behind the head is most brilliantly radiant. (He lets out a shout. Entering the hall, he said:
"Though a sharp sword is keen, it does not slay those who have committed no crime. Though sturdy bamboo is tall, it cannot point toward the moon at the edge of heaven.
Linji’s Three Mysteries and Dongshan’s Five Ranks—what idle household utensils are these?"
After a long silence, he said: "This too is for the sake of others, increasing ignorance through idle matters.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The wind does not come, the tree does not move; the mind does not arise, the object does not arrive.
A monk asked Yunmen, "What is the Buddha? Yunmen said, "A dry dung pellet. A monk asked Yangqi, "What is the Buddha? Yangqi said, "A three-legged donkey."
The colt prances its hooves as it walks; a fine assembly! Previously on the road, he was called a dragon, yet none believed him. Indeed, he has now won the silken banner and returned.

Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Chan Master Huanglong Xin, who engaged in an intense discussion with Xia Gongli on the *Zhao Lun* (Treatise on Emptiness), debating how all phenomena arise from the One Mind.
"Self and others, the sentient and the insentient, are of one body. At that time, there was a dog lying beneath a fragrant table.
Yunlong picked up his measuring scale and struck the dog; he then struck the fragrant table and said, "The dog is sentient and has departed;
the table is insentient and remains here. How can the sentient and the insentient become one body? Gongli was unable to offer a rebuttal. Yunlong said, "Just as..."
To engage in discursive thought is to create superfluous dharmas; when has one ever realized that the myriad things are oneself?
The old man Huanglong’s compassion was not lacking in his lament. Master Xia Gongli entered a mountain of treasures and returned empty-handed.
If you all wish to realize that the myriad things are yourself, are sentient and insentient beings of one body? Hammer to death the dog with feelings! Smash it to pieces!
Take this insentient incense table and pack it up with all your might; bind it into a single bundle and cast it into the vast eastern ocean, where it will naturally become free and unencumbered.
Nevertheless, you must further know that there is a single aperture at the crown of the head before you have attained it.
Holding up his staff and striking the incense altar, he said: "Alala! Alala! Climbing the mountain, my knees ache; sipping tea, my tongue slips.
At the crossroads stands the Stone Gaṇdang; facing the moon and the wind, he blows his flute."

Ascending the hall, he said: "In the morning you contemplate the *Prajñāpāramitā*, in the evening you recite the *Avataṃsaka*. Not a single character has ever been spoken; how could it cut off the myriad differences?
It stands like a sheer cliff ten thousand fathoms high. As for your own self, how could you have ever realized it? A snake does not move without a head; a tiger runs only when it has feet."
The old barbarian Bodhidharma—his face is three inches thick! He ascends the hall:
The morning sun shines upon the high crags, a brilliant, golden-yellow hue. Samantabhadra shrinks his head and hides his body;
Mañjuśrī exerts his great majestic power. All you people sit on the ground watching Yangzhou; this mountain monk also sits on the ground watching Yangzhou. Ox.
The horns of a ram are three inches long; the horns of a rabbit are eight feet long.
Entering the hall: Lingyun saw the peach blossoms; Xiangyan heard the striking of the bamboo. His eyes and ears emitted a great radiance.
It illuminates and penetrates all things, yet it alone cannot illuminate itself. If it were able to illuminate itself, it would not be the original light.
[Ascending the hall: Just now, when the attendant struck the drum, each stroke struck the very heart and five viscera of you all.
"Do you still feel the pain? Now this elder speaks of yellow and black; every single word he utters reaches the spirits of seven generations within your own household.
Do you know how to feel shame? If you do indeed recognize this, it may be said that the kindness is too great to be repaid."
If you still do not understand, I shall not fail to provide you with another footnote. [The Master] picks up his staff, strikes it once, and ascends the hall to address the assembly:
"Zen practitioners say, 'There is nothing we do not know; there is nothing we do not understand. Yet when someone suddenly asks, 'What is the matter of traveling for practice?
their mouths hang open like a flat eaves. Where does the sickness lie? It lies in having too much knowledge and too many explanations."
Studying the Way in such a manner is not as good as being a farmer in a village of three households. Suppose someone were to ask, "How are the crops this year?
One could explain every detail, like water pouring from a jar. This is because such a person lacks intellectual understanding and lacks the need for discrimination.
As the autumn air grows cold, each of you should return to your hall. Take care.

Ascending the hall, he raised the following case: "Whenever it was time for the midday meal, Nanyue Jinniu would personally carry the food to the front of the Sangha Hall and perform a dance, calling out, 'Sons of the Buddha, come and eat!
The Master commented: 'Jinniu exposed his own ugly behavior; who would be willing to eat such left-over soup and rancid rice? "
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "The school of direct pointing has from the beginning no separate dharma; it simply requires that each person bring themselves to completion.
Yet the descendants of later generations speak of the void while riding upon the void, twisting the straight into the crooked—this is what is meant by writing the character for 'nine' as 'bird'."
Hutou wrote [the character for] "emperor" three times and thereby became an emperor; Lingyan could not become a human being—he was merely a fellow who eats and defecates.
You all must not recklessly create artificial complications.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Lu Zu saw a monk and faced the wall; Juṭi saw a monk and raised a finger. There was pointing and there was non-pointing.

Xuefeng overturned the rice bucket; Ganji prostrated before the steamer. Whether these are essential points or not—once you involve discursive thought, you have already entered the realm of the shadows. He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The entire world of the ten directions is a single sword. Tell me, in whose hands does the hilt and grip fall?
Even if you can explain it clearly, I must ask you: is this a sword that kills, or a sword that gives life?"

Ascending the hall, he said: “To clarify one’s capacity is to savor it for oneself; to cease mental activity is to lose the source. To turn the head or twist the brain is to fall into pits and ravines.
The Patriarch said: ‘The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing. Simply do not harbor hatred or love, and you will see clearly and brightly.
How many people has this driven to distraction? How many people has it paralyzed?”

Ascending the hall for the ceremony of re-skinning the Dharma drum, he simply dismissed them as they were; it was already three *kē* late. Why then point east and draw west, or speak of yellow and describe black?
Even those with clear eyes will have cause to grit their teeth. Nevertheless, where there is a branch, one grasps it; where there is no branch, one follows the precedent.
Have you not seen how Yanguan addressed the assembly: "Take empty space as the drum and Mount Sumeru as the mallet. What kind of person [can strike it]?"
[He] struck it. [Then he] dug a hole and buried it deep. Nanquan said, "Master Wang does not strike this broken drum;

this is a case of the refined recognizing the refined. Fayen Bie remarked, "Master Wang does not strike it; this is like whetting one's axe at the gate of Ban Qu. Lingyan has newly stretched the skin over the Dharma-drum."
Using wood for a body and leather for a face, one may strike when one wishes to strike and cease when one wishes to cease;
there is no such fuss as this. It is simply that one must not hear it. To hear it is to lose one's body and life. But who is it that loses body and life?
The rotting straw sandals beneath the bed, and the bald broom of reeds at the base of the fence.
Ascending the hall: "One Ding, two Zhuo. There are thorns in the soft mud. "Release two, cast three. Auspiciousness without anything not favorable.
Before the hall, the iron saw dances the Three Platforms; casually, it shatters the crown of the skull.
Ascending the hall, he said: "A mad elephant is difficult to tame; a withered stump is easy to pull. The pearl of the Sui dynasty is no treasure;
fish eyes produce a false glow. *Du-du-du!* With all my might! Who would trade a golden bullet for your dung ball?"

Ascending the hall, he said: "A great staff strikes empty space; even empty space does not feel the pain through to its core. The old Gautama of the Yellow Face has blood flowing from the crown of his head.
Seeking to have his grievances known, he preached for forty-nine years. The lantern serves as witness, and the pillar becomes loquacious. A-he-he!
He topples the great mountain at the gate and then reaches for the bright moon from within the fire."
Ascending the hall, he said: "A sparrow does not defecate upon the head of a hawk; one with clear eyes does not ask a blind person for directions;
empty flowers cannot bear fruit; and a mirage cannot quench thirst. These four matters are known by all people."
Because the Dharma is thus. The World-Honored One said: "The Dharma is fundamentally no-Dharma; no-Dharma is also Dharma.
Now, when transmitting no-Dharma, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?"
Xie Guoqing, the Abbot of Qingliang Temple and the Tripitaka Master of Kaiyuan, ascends the hall and says: "The one path that points upward has not been transmitted by the thousand sages;
even before one has set foot upon it, one is already separated from it by a great trichiliocosm. Within Qingliang Mountain, ten thousand bodhisattvas drag plows and pull harrows;
in Fangguang Monastery, the Venerable Banzhian serves as the ritual attendant for the midday meal. Only the stone Buddha of Kaiyuan remains stubbornly steadfast."
The ground: the wind cannot enter it; the water cannot wet it. More than five thousand scrolls, each word different, have come from the dragon palaces and the ocean treasuries.
Entering the hall: there is neither past nor present, neither odor nor sound. Above heaven and below heaven, none can rival it. The frog.
Earthworms. Possessing the ten marks in full. Wooden roosters and straw dogs. Chanting the Way and discussing the sutras—let out a shout!
This is still half a month’s journey behind Lingyan.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Surging waves and boiling cauldrons—arising, one must be entirely true. Silent stillness and non-action—lead back to the realm of emptiness. Cutting off both extremes, there is a world of radiant brilliance. To mistake a thief for one's own son is to plunder one’s family wealth. He took up his staff, drew a line, and said: [The Master] ascended the hall. "Waves surging and cauldrons boiling:

when arising, one must be entirely true. Silent and inactive: lead back to the realm of emptiness. Cut off both ends; there is a world of radiant glory. To mistake a thief for one's own son is to rob one's family of its assets. He took up his staff, drew a line, and said:
On the three borders there is no need for spears or armor; ten thousand miles away, songs of joy celebrate the Great Peace. Entering the hall, he said:
"Leaving kin behind and severing attachments, shaving the head and donning the dyed robes—having entered this gate, what should one do?

If you possess a sense of shame and a recognition of propriety, you are a true renunciant. First, you have departed from the mundane world and the home of affectionate ties; second, you have departed from the fires of the triple realm."
To dwell in the house. Third, one leaves the house of coarse delusions and afflictions. Fourth, one leaves the house of subtle delusions and ignorance.

Having left these four houses, one may for the first time be called a member of the *nanseng* (patch-robed monk) family. Now, what is the *nanseng* family? It is where you encounter an adversary; it is the petty home of foul-mouthed abuse.
Ascending the hall: The stone woman sings aloud as she passes before; the wooden man claps his hands in response.
An ant seizes the great wind-wheel, and billions of Mount Sumerus are tossed and shaken.
A Confucian scholar and a Daoist priest came to visit; the Master ascended the hall, held up his whisk, and said: "The sages of the Three Teachings are all present upon the tip of this whisk.
They entwine branches and extend tendrils, discoursing on the wondrous and discussing the profound. The Confucianist says: 'My Way is unified by a single thread.'"
The elder said, "The Sage embraces the One and serves as a model for the world. The Buddhist said, "There is only this one reality;
all else is not true. Since each has their own justification, they cannot avoid competing for strength and weakness.

How, then, shall we judge them so that their voices may harmonize and their echoes accord, so that forms may be straight and shadows upright? Break down the fences of self and other, and block [the flow of delusion].
The cave of ignorance. [He] strikes the whisk. Two arise from one; do not cling even to that one. At midday, he strikes the third watch;
facing south, he gazes at the Big Dipper.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "If one is deluded, one is entirely deluded; if one awakens, one is entirely awakened. When awakening, one awakens to that which was deluded; when deluded, one is deluded regarding that which is awakened.
Delusion and awakening, awakening and delusion, are like water meeting water, or fire meeting fire. Throughout kalpas past and present, they have never been anything other than this."
Ascending the hall: "In the morning one ascends the hall; in the evening one enters the room. What business has this with the bustling gate and courtyard?
When Deshan beckoned from across the river, Gaoting simply strode straight across. When Magu took up his hoe and entered the garden, Liangshui immediately ceased all activity.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Cutting off the path of birth and death, one sits loftily atop the city of nirvana. As for a defeated general, how could his merits be worth discussing?
Racing horses upon Mount Sumeru, picking up a lamp beneath the bottom of the great ocean—to raise such an instance is easy; to comprehend it is difficult."

Upon ascending the hall for the ceremony of thanking the Supervisor of Revenues, Lai Su Zhuang, the mountain monk said: "Yesterday, I dispatched several veteran generals to subdue those who have not yet submitted.

Since they awaited my arrival, they were brought down in a single drum-roll. Truly, the winds blew at the proper time and the rains fell at the proper time; the fine grains ripened and the common people rejoiced.
Now, as we withdraw the army and celebrate our victory, discussing merits and enjoying a time of peace, I shall sit here in contemplation. Thus it was said.
Lord Bi could not restrain his joy; unconsciously, his hands began to dance and his feet to leap.
Upon the tip of a single hair, he raised his voice and sang: "Xian Gao Yi-bo of Taizhou, Red lotus, green river-mouth, white.
The shrimp-shell returns to the Lianzi-lattice. Tell me, what tune is this? It is simply: 'When one's meal is finished, one plays with the chopsticks.'"
Winter Solstice Small Sermon: The sea temple lies desolate; crags and peaks cluster like an archway. Beyond the gate, the cold tide soaks the moon;

before the courtyard, ancient trees shriek in the wind. Everyone sees this with their eyes and hears it with their ears; every single thing transcends the present and surpasses the past. One quiets the mysterious mechanism before its signs appear;
one conceals the dark operation within the very process of transformation. As Ciming posted his notice before the hall, Dongshan applied the hexagram to the Gate of Ghosts.

He clears away the fruit table. To deceive and ensnare ordinary people—if it were not for the clear illumination of the eye of wisdom, all would be taken as marvelous talk and intellectual understanding.
Therefore it is said: "In practicing Chan, one must penetrate the barrier of the Patriarchs; in studying the Way, one must exhaust the path of the mind.

If the path of the mind is not exhausted and the barrier of the Patriarchs is not penetrated, one will inevitably still be subject to the shifts of cold and heat and remain enshrouded by birth and death. (He raises his staff.)
[The Master] said: "This land is one hundred thousand *li* west of India. On the winter solstice and the Cold Food Festival on the one-hundred-and-fifth day, [the seasons change].
Again, he cited: When Guishan addressed the assembly, he said, 'The bitter cold of mid-winter is an annual occurrence; as the movement of the sun’s shadow shifts, what is the nature of this matter?
Yangshan stepped forward and stood with his hands clasped. Guishan said, 'I also know that you cannot answer this question. However—"
[Guishan] asked Xiangyan, "How do you understand this? Xiangyan said, "I am particularly able to answer this question.

He then crossed his hands and stepped forward to stand. Guishan said, "Fortunately, Jizi does not understand. *Commentary:* Guishan was about to lead his two disciples toward a time when the ice is frozen and the snow is deep, hosting a banquet for the entire family.
With bear paws and camel humps, they set down their chopsticks in weary satiety; the pipes and strings [of music]...
The *tuo* drum resounds, its sound piercing the clouds and reaching the heavens; those who behold it from near or afar cannot help but be filled with admiration.

Yet, when it comes to the distribution of family property, they remain as divided as the states of Wu and Yue. (He strikes the whisk. At first, I thought it was merely that the thatch was uneven; having cut it down, I find the ground itself is not level.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The mind is like a skilled performer; the intellect is like the conductor of the performance; the five consciousnesses are its companions; and deluded thoughts watch the spectacle.
Does the great assembly still recognize the mind? If you recognize the mind, you will recognize the intellect;

if you recognize the intellect, you will recognize the various consciousnesses; if you recognize the various consciousnesses, you will recognize deluded thoughts. When deluded thoughts are extinguished, then all [phenomena]..."
Consciousness ceases. When all consciousnesses cease, the mind (*manas*) ceases. When the mind ceases, the heart-mind (*citta*) ceases. When the heart-mind ceases, everything ceases. Thus it is said:
"When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise; when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. (He lets out a shout.
What fault is there in the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars? Descend from your seat.

Ascending the Dharma Hall on New Year’s Day: At the beginning of the new year, the Buddha-dharma is manifest everywhere. Guests arriving in throngs to celebrate the year receive a cordial welcome with their shoes pulled off in haste.
Laughing, he points to the fine weather; wind and sun remain mild and bright. "The fields and rice will surely ripen," he says, "and we shall sing of peace with full bellies.
The assembly: "If a superior person suddenly arrives, how would you attend to them? Qingyuan: [Silence]
Wine. Zhaozhou’s tea. Three cups, two goblets, and one sleeps drunk amidst the mists and clouds. For the most part, such is the free-flowing style of those who uphold the lineage.

On the occasion of the Lantern Festival, the Abbot was invited to ascend the hall by the Rear Hall Head. "A single bowl of lamp-light from vast kalpas past— How many have known it to illuminate heaven and earth?
If you wish to see where the transmission is inexhaustible, It is when one awakens from the dream within the Tuṣita Palace."

May the Abbot assemble the congregation to perform the Liang Emperor’s Repentance and request that he ascend the seat. The adamantine true body is like empty space: in heaven it is as heaven, on earth it is as earth.
It gives birth to the myriad existents and encompasses all things from antiquity to the present. It melts stones and liquefies gold yet remains without heat;
it cracks glue and causes fingers to fall off yet remains without cold. It rises far above the entanglements of existence and utterly transcends words and meanings. As for what occurred previously...

If one can grasp this inwardly and carry it forth, and comprehend it so as to put it into practice, then one will see that Qi Shi was a serpent-body yet realized the Dharma-body, and Emperor Wu of Liang understood worldly wisdom yet clarified true wisdom.

Whether they be monastics or laypeople, men or women, those in the unseen realm or the manifest world, the holy or the ordinary—there is no sin to repent, for sins melt away like ice; there is no merit to cultivate, for merit... [is spontaneously perfected].
Reaching the same river, there is no kindness that goes unrequited, no wish that is not fulfilled, no fruit that is not realized, and no practice that is not perfected.

Every thing is subsumed within it; every dharma is perfectly interfused. Their lights intermingle and entwine like a net of precious jewels. Whether in heaven or in hell, one wanders freely according to one's own nature;
amidst mountains of fire and peaks of knives, one appears and disappears at will. Moving left or right, there is nothing that is not acceptable. Directly...
A thousand auspicious signs gather in profusion; ten thousand virtues arrive in their entirety. Qilin appear and phoenixes manifest; weapons are laid aside and civil virtue is cultivated.
Autumn grain ripens and the common people rejoice. Although it is thus, where does the ultimate merit finally reside?
(He strikes the whisk. The imperial wind fans forever; the Buddha-sun shines eternally bright.
Again, he spoke in verse: "Excellent, O Great Being! Your name is Shan-yuan (Good Vow). Your vow is lofty and profound; neither mountain nor sea can serve as its metaphor.

Out of compassion for this world of five turbidities, where sentient beings are entangled in afflictions and have long accumulated the stains of transgression—stains that cannot be cleansed except through repentance—I recall the sovereign of the Liang dynasty, when the Xi clan monopolized the inner harem. Their deluded attachment was as firm as glue and lacquer; [even] at death..."

In life, we constantly face one another; yet due to anger, we fall into the class of pythons. Suffering, we pray for deliverance; only then do we realize that we were deluded and turned our backs on awakening. Everywhere we form attachments;
yet where there is no mind, there is no transgression, and where there is a mind, there is still transgression. I pay homage to those holy masters to initiate this "Mindless Repentance.
Their bequeathed writings hang like the sun and moon, illuminating all beneath them for a thousand years. For all who follow and practice them, there is no [further suffering].
Failing to obtain benefit, I have therefore, on this first day of the New Year, gathered a vast assembly of pure beings to proclaim this once more before the Buddha.

Like snow melting in boiling water, my accumulated sins are cleansed. Within the various oceans of the Flower Treasury (*Gandavyūha*) and the oceans of diverse expressions—whether explained extensively or concisely, or taught in their totality—this meaning is inexhaustible;
its merit is likewise endless. I universally pray that all sentient beings may [attain liberation]. I vow...
Exerting the power of great repentance, he ascended the hall and cited a verse by Master Fu Dashi: "Holding a hoe in empty hands, *gate gate*;
Walking while riding a water buffalo, *pāragate*; A person passes over the bridge, *pārasaṃgate*; The bridge flows, yet the water does not."
[The Master] descends from his seat. He ascends the hall.
He cites a monk’s question to Xianglin: “What is the single lamp within the room? Xianglin replied, “Three people testify that a tortoise becomes a turtle.
[The Master] comments: “Three people testify that a tortoise becomes a turtle; each has a tongue in its mouth. When the opportunity arises, one must not...”

Discerning the wind that comes: even when drinking water, one must guard against choking. Old Xianglin was able to lift up the true lamp to illuminate the world, yet now it has been blown out by all. *He lets out a shout.*
Nirvana ascends the hall: "This morning is the fifteenth day of the second month; it causes people to exhaust their very entrails.

Shushan’s wooden snake in his hand bites to death the fierce tiger of the South Mountain. Turning over, he strikes through empty space—a masterful feat that would be difficult even for a skilled craftsman to repair."
"Beating one's breast is only fit for weeping to the blue heavens. To trigger the mechanism, one must have a crossbow capable of launching a thousand-jin bolt.
[He] struck the meditation seat and ascended the hall. "The spring days linger long; the spring flowers blaze forth. The Great Matter is manifest before us, yet ordinary minds do not perceive it.

If you were to perceive it, you would transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts, transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers, and transform afflictions..."
For the sake of Bodhi, one turns ignorance into Great Wisdom. If one does not awaken, one will continue to rise and sink within the sea of birth and death.
To speak in this way is to accommodate the needs of the present age. Do you all feel the heaviness upon the crown of your heads?
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "For those who come this way, I cut off their heels; for those who do not come this way, I pierce their nostrils.

Setting aside for a moment 'this way' and 'not this way,' last night Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra gave rise to views of Buddha and views of Dharma, so I gave each of them twenty blows and banished them to the two Iron Encircling Mountains.
If people know this, tell me: what of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception today?"
“How many people have abdicated their positions in a single day?

[The Master] gave a shout. He ascended the hall and said: “The mind has no inherent nature; it manifests entirely through phenomena. Phenomena have no intrinsic substance; they appear entirely through the mind.
At times, one takes a single blade of grass and makes it the sixteen-foot golden body of the Buddha. At other times, one takes the sixteen-foot golden body and makes it a single blade of grass.”
Seven out, eight in; struck here, struck there. Before the Hall of Bright Moon, jade dew hangs down; within the Palace of Crystal, true pearls are scattered.
Entering the hall [he says]: "The single, firm, and dense body manifests within all dust motes. He picks up his staff and says: "Śākyamuni the Old Man has arrived!"
Furthermore, from each of his three hundred and sixty joints and eighty-four thousand pores, he emits great rays of light that illuminate lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Within these realms, whether they be sages or ordinary beings, sentient or insentient, all who are touched by this light realize Great Nirvana, attain Great Peace and Bliss, and achieve Great Enjoyment. At this moment, leaning upon his staff—
If you do not investigate the root source, you must simply wait for the future to question Maitreya.
Addressing the assembly on a spring day: In this deep spring at the mountain temple, the grasses and trees flourish. How many times have I intentionally opened the wooden gate?
The traveler remains only beyond the green mountains; The cuckoo calls out its name, yet he does not return.
Ascending the hall: At the pork table and beneath the funeral curtain, the assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly as if it had not yet dispersed.
Panshan has no principle to extend; Zhiyi has no subtlety to speak. Eyes like wooden stakes; mouths like drum mallets.
Ascending the hall on the Buddha’s birthday: Before the Yellow-Faced Old Man had even emerged from his mother’s womb, he was a man of great power.
Once he was born, however, his mouth began to chatter; it became quite unbearable.

When he said, “In the heavens above and the earth below, I alone am honored,” it was like throwing a brick in a bustling marketplace—it was bound to hit someone. Yet, alas, there was no one to take it up.
Descend from your seats.

This is the small *cankuan* (general address) for the summer retreat. Those who are sharp and quick should lift their robes and go; they are like a hawk snatching a pigeon—thirty blows to the heels would be well-deserved.
Those who are dull and confused do not turn back even after three attempts; they are like fish in a stagnant pond—a single needle-point on the crown of their heads would suffice.

Throughout the heavens and earth of past and present, throughout the sun and moon of past and present, and throughout the human relations of past and present—what is good does not increase by a single hair’s breadth, and what is ugly does not decrease by a single hair’s breadth.
To take Great Perfect Enlightenment as one’s monastery, yet to draw lines on the ground to create a prison, is where the terminology of punishment becomes manifest.
While body and mind dwell in peace within the wisdom of equality, they remain buried in the ghost cave of delusion, where worldly anxieties abound. Tomorrow, at Lingyan Temple...
The Summer Retreat begins. Tonight’s small discourse (*xiaocan*) will neither involve eloquent talk nor profound mysteries, nor will it establish any fixed schedule or limits.
Beneath the three-beam roof and before the seven-foot mat, let each person sleep as they please—lying down or rolling over—and eat when hungry and drink when thirsty.

You may be certain that the flower of the mind will then blossom and illuminate the lands of the ten directions. Should you, however, harbor thoughts of limitation or fall into the trap of mere views and hearing, then at another time...
On a later day, someone came to collect the fee for the meal. [The Master] said, "Do not say that I did not tell you.
He further raised this case: When the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma in the kingdom of Magadha, it was near the end of the summer retreat.

He then said to Ānanda, "Among the great disciples and the fourfold assembly of devas and humans, I have constantly preached the Dharma, yet they do not give rise to reverence or admiration. I shall now enter..."

While dwelling in his old room during the ninety-day summer retreat, a person suddenly came to inquire about the Dharma. "Speak on my behalf," he said, "that all dharmas are unborn and all dharmas are unceasing.
Having spoken these words, he closed his room and sat in silence. The verse says: The white summer retreat is drawing to a close; May you show compassion and persevere in your cultivation.
If humans and devas do not look up with reverence, Time and months will simply pass away. Dharma after dharma is without...
Arising and ceasing—every single thing involves letting go and gathering in. For these ninety days, I have merely closed my door; this great kindness is truly difficult to repay.
On the occasion of the Summer Retreat, Yunmen ascended the hall and said: "The fifteenth day of this month marks the beginning of the summer retreat. What do you say, Hanshan?"
The Way of Lingyan: this month’s fifteenth marks the commencement of summer retreat. How is it with the black lacquer bucket?
A sandalwood grove is surrounded by sandalwood; a lion’s den is surrounded by lions. The nostrils of the patch-robed monk hang down low;
behind the diamond-hard skull is three catties of iron.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The void arises within Great Awakening, like a single bubble surfacing upon the ocean. The minute dust-motes of lands with outflows are all born dependent upon the void.
These lands are born dependent on the void; the void is born dependent on Great Awakening. Great Awakening has nothing upon which it depends; this is called the Treasury of Radiance.

Suddenly, amidst the assembly, there was a monk who, relying on the literal text to explain the meaning, displayed the family style of a lecture master—shifting his grasp from east to west and dodging from side to side. At that time...

Flowing toward [the goal], yet among the ranks of patch-robed monks, I have not yet seen a true master. When I, this mountain monk, heard such words spoken, I was moved to prostrate myself headlong in worship.
Why? I had thought there were only white monkeys; now I see there are also black ones.

Ascending the hall for the inauguration of the Imperial Birthday, he held up his staff and said: "Its loftiness is unsurpassed; its vastness is boundless. This is what is called the Sage among Sages, the Heaven among Heavens.
He drives the three luminaries to shine upon all, and governs the myriad realms to illuminate the world. There is none who does not submit without thought;
there is no response that is not immediately communicated. He struck the staff and said: "He cleaves apart Mount Hua, revealing its celestial splendor, and lets forth the Yellow River..."
The river is thoroughly clear.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "When meeting, one does not bring it forth; as soon as the intention is raised, one knows it exists. Casting down the piece of firewood, there is no small amount of self-display."
Fined money, he leaves the monastery; his strength exhausted at the Wu River. Upon the mountain there is a carp; at the bottom of the well there is dust from the pines.
Within a peach pit of a thousand years, what trace of its former kernel can one find?

Ascending the hall, he said: "The karma of the great assembly cannot be contrived, nor can it be avoided. Have you not heard the Way? 'Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten.
The World-Honored One received the retribution of the golden spear and the horse-barley; Kāśyapa received the retribution of golden color for every lifetime.
Yet these two types of retribution have no characteristic of arising and no characteristic of ceasing; they are like wind blowing over water, naturally forming [ripples]."
The Text:
At the conclusion of the ritual, he ascends the hall and says: "In the year of three hundred and sixty days, this day alone is most auspicious.
When the Yellow River clears, a sage emerges; with civil classics as warp and military strategy as woof, the Hall of Enlightenment is opened. Once the sage has emerged, all under heaven is at peace."

Govern by non-action; let it be done without being commanded. The dust of the south and north is entirely swept away; the myriad people sing of the Yellow Emperor and the Duke of Tang in joyful harmony.
Ascending the hall: there is no need to lower your head; it is difficult to find through deliberation. Bodhi and affliction are like the sound of a hot bowl [clinking]. For example:
Refining iron into an implement: it is red when entering the fire and black when emerging from the fire; the nature of the iron remains as before. Entering the Hall:
Perfectly clear and aware, not dependent on mental thought—vivid and agile, it covers the earth and covers the heavens.
Cast away the seven and the three and preserve the one; closing one’s eyes, one leaps over the Yellow River. Waiting for the sun to rise at dusk.
Ascending the hall on the Double Fifth: On the fifth day of the fifth month, the Duanwu Festival, racing boats compete by the riverbanks while songs and pipes resound.
Monks together sip calamus tea; infinite fragrance arises upon their lips and tongues. A hundred ailments are eliminated; a thousand demons are utterly extinguished.
Mañjuśrī ordered Sudhana to gather medicinal herbs. Sudhana picked up some grass and handed it to Mañjuśrī, who planted it upon a rock where flowers immediately sprouted.
Mañjuśrī received them and showed them to the assembly, saying, "This medicine can both kill people and bring them back to life. He then drove a wooden stake into the air.
Looking around to his left and right, he said, "Is there anyone who can act as a host for Mañjuśrī and Sudhana?
He gave a shout. Then, ascending the hall, he cited the teachings which say: "Ordinary people truly claim it exists; those of the Two Vehicles analyze it and claim it does not exist;
Perfect Enlightenment calls it illusory existence; Bodhisattvas realize its very substance is emptiness. He then remarked: "A tiger bites a tiger; a snake swallows a turtle's nose."

Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the fifteenth day, it is like a precipice marking the way or a mountain peak standing firm; after the fifteenth day, it is like lightning flashing and thunder rolling.
On the fifteenth day itself, the wind does not rustle the branches, and the rain does not break the clods of earth.

Holding up his staff, he said: "This staff has long kept this essential point in silence, not seeking to speak of it hastily. Now that humans and devas have gathered here and the Buddha-work flourishes, it simply must be revealed."
Come forth! Reveal a bit of news. Alas, it has fallen into the hands of Lingyan; if you want to lean it horizontally, you cannot; if you want to stand it vertically, you cannot.
Nevertheless, to grasp it is to lose the proper measure and inevitably enter a deviant path; to let it go naturally, its substance has neither going nor staying.
Then, holding his staff horizontally, he said: "Right now it is horizontal. Within the trichiliocosm, sentient beings and..."
Sentient beings—without exception—are covered and obscured by it. [The Master] raises [his staff] and says: "Right now it is upright.

Reaching upward to the summit of Mount Sumeru and downward to the edge of the golden wheel and the waters, sentient and non-sentient beings alike are all obstructed and hindered by it. [The Master] lifts it up and says:
"Right now it is neither horizontal nor upright. The *śakara* eye cannot see it; the thousand hands of Great Compassion cannot touch it."
The thousand Buddhas who appear in the world cannot exhaustively praise him; Māra, with all his kin assembled, cannot disparage him.
Great Assembly, this staff possesses such spiritual powers and such wondrous functions that it is fitting for it to appear and vanish, to roll up and unfold, attaining great mastery.
Why was it just now so hesitant and withdrawn? And why does it now possess such brilliance? Have you not heard it said: "It is attained from..."
The mind: it makes the *eranda* tree into a sandalwood tree; it loses its essence in its aim. Nectar becomes a garden of thorns.
Strike once more! [He descends from his seat.]
Ascending the hall, [the Master said: "Before the time of Vipaśyin, there was fundamentally no transmission or reception. After Śākyamuni, it has been handed down and maintained in succession.
Melting together vases, plates, hairpins, and bracelets, they become a single gold; churning butter, cream, and clarified butter, they become a single flavor. Master Linji said:
'Who knew that my Treasury of the True Dharma Eye would be extinguished at the hands of that blind donkey? One only knows that opening one's mouth is easy, but fails to realize—"
The tongue is long.
As Master Ruyong Mengtang ascended the hall for the morning service: "A great person possesses great vision; one of great wisdom attains great function.
With a black-lacquered bamboo whisk, he overturns the seas and mountains; with a *bājiǎo* staff, he strikes at empty space. It reaches the point where even Śākyamuni..."
Shi Le folded his hands in submission. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra had nowhere left to hide their bodies. Therefore it is said: "To kill a person, one must have the sword that kills;
to give life to a person, one must have the sword that gives life. If you have the sword that gives life but lack the sword that kills, no living person can die.
If you have the sword that kills but lack the sword that gives life, no dead person can live."
To live as a dead man and die as a living man—even so, one still falls into the trap of merit and fame, burying the essential principle. Have you not seen?
One day, Master Fuyong visited his fellow student, Master Shixing. Shixing then ascended the hall, took his staff in his right hand, leaned it against the left side, and after a long silence, said:
"If this matter had not been entrusted to my elder brother Fuyong, it would have been most difficult."
"Understand this thoroughly," he said, and then descended from his seat. When Shixing spoke thus, Li Xiang bit into the red edge.
In these present times, one must bare the shoulders to carry the burden and hold it up with bare hands; without falling into triviality, one must cut through nails and sever iron.

There is only my elder brother, Master Ruilong, who does so. Do not say that the land is vast and the people few, and keep this secret without revealing it. I only wish that you would loosen the thread of the path.

To comply entirely with the exigencies of the times, those who merely receive the words and remain stuck on the phrases will now clearly realize the direct pointing and the single transmission—this wondrously upheld Great Matter.
Is this not truly appropriate? The assembly, including the *xiàzuò* and the *shǒuzuò*, together prostrate and make this request, hoping that you will propagate it.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Buddha to Buddha, hand to hand; Patriarch to Patriarch, transmitted from one to another. Steaming sand will never produce rice; digging the earth makes it difficult to find heaven.

Patriarch to Patriarch, transmitted from one to another; Buddha to Buddha, hand to hand. A dull bird flies against the wind; a shrimp leaps but cannot escape the measuring basket. If it can leap out, all matters are finished;
if it cannot leap out, it must endure its humiliation. A barefooted Persian enters the Great Tang—what a pair of eyes!"
The pupils of his eyes dart about like crows.

He ascends the hall to pray for rain, yet the sweet rain has missed its appointed time; the fields are cracked open like tortoise shells. The nostrils of this patch-robed monk are parched with heat, and smoke rises from them.
He held up his staff and said, "The staff has transformed into a dragon and is now departing for the southern Jambudvīpa to bring down rain.
This mountain monk cannot simply wash his hands and let it go; I must lend my spiritual power to assist it. He struck the ground with the staff and said, "Swift as a decree!
*Ji-jí rú lù-ling. Chì*!"
Ascending the hall after successfully praying for rain, [the Master] said: "A single thought of faith arises, and all Buddhas are able to know it.
Holding up his staff, he said: "The Buddhas are here; where is the faith? Yesterday we burned incense and prayed, and this morning a torrential downpour came.
It cooled the feverish afflictions and revived the withered sprouts. [He drew a line on the staff: "This is not what was moved by faith."
It is not that the Buddhas have descended as spirits. If you understand this, you have been deceived by me;
if you do not understand it, there is porridge and rice upon the long beds.

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Upon this lump of red flesh there is something—vivid and lucid, yet hazy and indistinct; it adapts and transforms according to circumstances, entirely free from constraint.
If you wish to know its place of origin clearly, it is not separate from the lifting and lowering of your feet.
Nowadays, when brothers in the monastic community hear such talk, they immediately say it is 'old woman’s Zen. Yet they do not realize that the clouds have no mind."
It emerges from the mountain clefts; water fills its basins and flows, yet it must stop upon encountering a high mountain, resting only when reaching the great ocean.
[The Master] pats the meditation seat.
Head Seat Zhongfu and Abbot Yunzang ascend for the formal lecture. The wind blows and the grass bends; the water reaches and the channel forms. This is the true command.
Once set in motion, the ten directions are severed at their roots. Muzhou pressed people until their legs broke; Yunmen cast down a piece of firewood.
Though these were indeed cases of transcending the school and surpassing the norm, they could not avoid being wrapped in hemp and paper. They are worthy of laughter; they are worthy of sorrow.
As for the matter of meeting atop Mount Wushan—once the one who knows it knows it, who else can know?

Small-scale *chanshi* (private instruction) for the end of the summer retreat: If Bodhidharma had not come to this eastern land and the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven, then the water would rise as the boat rises, and the mud would be thick as the Buddha grows large.
