Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the realm of Ruiyan? The Master said, "The wind cannot enter. The monk asked, "Who is the person within the realm?
The Master said, "Water cannot wet him. The monk said, "I have already received the Master’s instruction on both the person and the realm."
"What is the matter regarding the vehicle of the ultimate lineage? The Master said, "The true does not conceal the false. The monk asked, "All phenomena are in a state of quiescent extinction;
why then do the banks move when a boat travels, and the moon appear to move as the clouds race by? The Master said, "What a wonderful message! I only fear you will misunderstand it."
The monk said, "A double-layered public case. The Master said, "The waters of the sea do not freeze into ice.
The Master then said, "Zhaozhou said, 'I cannot speak the Buddha-dharma to you at the latrine; one does not know the stench of one's own excrement.
Yunmen said, 'The Buddha-dharma is indeed abundant, it is only that the tongue is too short. How much more so! Longya asked Deshan, 'I have heard of Deshan from afar...'"
"A single phrase of the Buddha-dharma. When [the monk] arrived, he had never yet heard the Master speak a single phrase of the Buddha-dharma.

Deshan said, "What is there to dislike? A saw cutting a scale-beam. "I, too, have a phrase of the Buddha-dharma—a supreme pivot beyond the ordinary—which I shall now clearly bring forth and bestow upon the assembly. He then opened both hands and said, "Finished."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is the primary pivot? The Master said, "A frog chasing a hawk. The monk asked, "What is the final phrase?
The Master said, "A rat playing with a monkey. The monk said, "In that case, one goes out in seven ways and disappears in eight.
The Master said, "Do not pretend to have clarity. The monk said, "If a person lacks far-reaching foresight, they will surely..."
A monk said, "I have a lingering worry. The Master said, "In the early morning there is congee; at the time of the midday meal there is rice. What is there to worry about?

The monk said, "The shadows of bamboo sweep the steps, yet the dust does not stir; the moon pierces the bottom of the waves, yet the water leaves no trace. The Master said, "Two years under the same spring."
The monk lifted up his sitting mat and said, "I thank the Master for answering my question. The Master said, "The mouth is the gateway to calamity. The monk bowed.
The Master then said, "Ruigan has nothing to offer you all; there is only a bowl of mountain-field rice with unhusked grain.
You may eat it coarsely or chew it finely, but once you are full, you must stop. Within it, there is a single grain of sand—why is it that you cannot bite through it?"
[The Master] struck the seat. Suddenly, someone stepped forward and said, "I have bitten into it. The Master immediately told him, "You must spit it out at once!
When the Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, he ascended the hall and said, "The ancients said: 'The mind of *nirvāṇa* is easy to understand; the wisdom of differentiation is difficult to clarify.
To speak in such a way is laborious and fruitless. At the assembly for the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, the World-Honored One rubbed his chest with his hand and addressed the multitude, saying: 'You all...'"
"Observe well my body, the color of purple-polished gold. It exists today, but tomorrow it shall be no more.
Look upon it with full satisfaction; do not let yourself regret it later. Is there any great difference [between this and the following]? Master Yunmen held up his fan and said:
"The fan leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nostrils of Śakra. A carp of the Eastern Sea gives a single—"
“Strike! The rain pours down like a basin being overturned. What difference is there? [With his whisk, he draws a line and says: ‘When a man is poor, his wisdom is short;
when a horse is thin, its coat is long. One must know that beyond the distant mist and waves, there is another way of thinking.”
Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "Since this mountain monk entered the monastery, two months have already passed, yet it was as if only a single kṣaṇa had elapsed.
Within that interval, if one seeks the characteristic of even a single kṣaṇa, it is utterly unobtainable. Therefore it is said: 'The white mouse shifts and passes.'"
The Silver Terrace remains unchanged. You people, how do you conduct yourselves throughout the twelve hours of the day? When the mountains cut off doubt, there is no path;
when the stream turns back, there is yet another village.
Ascending the hall, he said: "If you wish to attain such a matter, you must be such a person. Since you are such a person, you need not worry about such a matter.
Raising the rhinoceros fan and casting out the thorny golden circle, one proclaims the ancestral wind of the Buddhas and patriarchs."
He opened the eyes and ears of the human and celestial realms. But what about that old woman to the east of the city, who was born at the same time as the Buddha yet did not wish to see him?
[The Master] strikes the whisk. "Two rows of tears upon the coral pillow; half are for thinking of you, half are for resenting you."
Ascending the hall for the opening ceremony: The Mind-King does not stir falsely, and the six realms are simultaneously penetrated.
Lay aside the three-foot sword; cease playing with the single bow. At this very moment, the Yellow River becomes crystal clear and the white sun radiates its brilliance.
The Golden Wheel is governed and the Jade Candle is harmonized; the Qilin appears and the Phoenix manifests. Throughout all under heaven, the Ultimate Way is employed.

I do not know. Beings who possess life receive the great creative force of existence yet offer no thanks. Furthermore, as for a man of the Way beneath the forest trees, how can he offer prayers of praise?
He raises his whisk and says: "Using only this true message, I reverently pray for the Emperor’s ten million years."
Kongzhao hesitated before offering incense. Before he had met Yantou, his mouth was like a foundation stone; once he had met Yantou, his eyes were like wooden stakes.
The fundamental principle supports the earth and props up the heavens—why labor over posing questions? Though the Master calls him and sends him away, he still lacks full alertness.
Inserting the incense, he said: "When meeting on the road, one does not dismount; each hastens toward their own future."

Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the scattering of offerings: The Dharma does not arise in isolation; it arises only by relying upon conditions. Today is the morning of the *parinirvāṇa* of the founding patriarch, Master Kōjō.
This mountain monk takes unspeakably, unspeakably many worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and makes them into a single banquet;
he takes ten billion Mount Sumerus and makes them into a single bowl of rice; he takes ten billion seas of fragrant water and makes them into...
"A single bowl of soup is briefly presented as an offering. At this very moment, where is this banquet spread?
If it were spread upon the world, since this world has already become the banquet, could there be another world outside of it?
If it were spread within empty space, empty space has no substantial form; furthermore, how could it..."
How shall it be arranged? If you simply leave it at that, you will again be indulging in a coarse understanding of Buddha-nature and a vague conception of True Suchness.
Is there anyone among this assembly who will come forward to take charge? If not, I, the old monk, shall handle it myself.

He brandishes the whisk. The worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, with their ten billion Mount Sumerus and ten billion fragrant seas—all the clusters of flowers and clusters of brocade—are spread out upon the tip of the whisk; neither too wide nor too narrow, without deficiency and without excess.
The great assembly, tell me: did the Patriarch Kongzhao accept this offering or not? Whether he accepted it or not, let that be for now;
where, do you say, does he dwell and establish his life at this very moment? [He] strikes the whisk. Before every door, the sun and moon blaze;
in an age of Great Peace, there is no need for the majesty of a general.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case: "Whenever Old Lu Zu saw a monk approach, he would simply sit with his face to the wall.

He remarked, 'The various quarters often offer wondrous and extraordinary interpretations, yet they fail to realize that this old monk has been branded on his face with the seal of no-character by others;
to this day, he does not wish to reveal it. Is there anyone here who, without moving a tongue, can vindicate him?"
After a long silence, there was only the moon shining on the wall, and not even a breeze blowing through the leaves.
He ascended the hall and said: "Before a single thought has arisen, you must by all means avoid clinging to this state.
Some say: 'The water flows cold from the side of the rock; the wind comes fragrant from within the flowers. I would strike such a fellow with my staff! It is autumn."
The moon shines upon the lofty hall; beneath the grass, the cricket chirps. Were it not for Zhong Ziqi, do not inquire after the subtleties within the lute.
[He] ascends the hall and says: "Venerable elders, there is form and there is light; there is mind and there are eyes. Empty the mind and exhaust form;
let the eyes have nothing to see and the light have nothing to receive. When inverted perceptions are extinguished, birth and death are like fire burning ice."

Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "That which cannot be seen is called 'the Plain' (Yi). Where, then, do the myriad phenomena of the universe find their repose? That which cannot be heard is called 'the Sparse' (Xi).
Amidst the clashing sounds of bells, fish-bells, drums, and wooden boards, where is it? That which cannot be grasped is called 'the Subtle' (Wei).
In putting on clothes and eating food, whose grace and power do you receive? Holding up his staff, he said: "Li Bo-yang (Laozi) rides a cow; enter into all of you!"
[He] went out through the eyes.
[The Master] ascended the hall and raised an example: Once, while serving a meal, Qingfeng asked Beiyuan, "The former master said: 'Grass plucked at random from the hand.'"

"Elder brother, how do you understand this? Beiyuan picked up a pair of chopsticks. Feng said, "If you understand it like that, when have you ever even dreamed of the late master? Beiyuan said, "If you understand it like that, when have you ever even dreamed of the late master? The Master commented: The elder brother asked, "How do you understand this? Beiyuan picked up a single chopstick.

Feng said, "If you understand it in this way, when have you ever dreamed of the late master? Beiyuan said, "If you understand it in this way, when have you ever dreamed of the late master? The Master commented:
One gain and one loss. Some may argue they have gained, yet it is not necessarily a good cause that brings about an evil result.
On the eighth day of the fourth month, ascending the hall: the bright pearl is in the palm; it divides its luster according to the various colors of the assembly.

The precious moon is in the sky; it manifests its reflection following the thousand rivers. [The Master] picks up his staff: "Old Śākyamuni is born! The nine dragons spit forth water to bathe the Golden One."

A body from which golden lotuses spring up from the earth supports his two feet; one with pupils in his eyes calls me a deceiver of the common folk, while one with no blood beneath his skin says I am using shrimp to catch turtles.
He plants his staff: when Guanyin buys a sesame cake, the Vajra Deity laughs himself to pieces.
A Small Sermon on Entering the Summer Retreat: The monastery of Perfect Enlightenment is fully possessed by every person.
In heaven, they are as heaven; on earth, they are as earth. Yet you all exert yourselves too much and cannot grasp it.

Therefore, the Tamer of Men from the Heaven of Śakra has toiled to open the gate of skillful means, establishing periods and limits—like forcing a living snake to transform into a dragon—to require that you personally realize and personally awaken.
Master Pang said: "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action (*wuwei*). This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return having passed the examination. Good assembly! An arrow does not miss its mark; when it is released, it must hit the center. My words do not miss their mark;
when they are released, they must be entirely true. I shall not ask about the needle-eyed fish swallowing the Great Elephant of Jiazhou; rather, let us speak of Master Ke.

"Three prostrations at the place where one attains the marrow—does this not also hit the mark? He struck the meditation seat. "The spring year has already ended; the terraces and pavilions are filled with lush green shade.
He then raised the case again: A monk asked Changqing, "In the long period of advancing on the Path, the Western Heaven uses a wax figure as a test. I wonder—"
"What is the proof for this? Changqing replied, "An iron ball. The monk asked, "What is the meaning of this? Changqing said, "The large ones are large;
the small ones are small. The Master commented, "Changqing’s response in this manner was like gazing at wild geese in the clouds and losing sight of the boat at the ferry crossing.
Every member of this assembly of mine considers themselves to be holding the pearl of the divine serpent."
"The raw jade of Mount Jing. Furthermore, when a mountain monk offers such a critique, is there anyone who remains unsatisfied? After a long silence:
"The mind that attempts to grasp it will ultimately find it difficult to comprehend; the adept should surely be startled in secret."

The next day he ascended the hall. A monk asked, "The Way is transmitted through words; transmission relies upon written characters. Without written characters, there would be nothing to record the words;
without words, how could the Way be revealed? Why, then, does the Master forbid people from reading and studying written texts?
The Master said, "A dog that bites on a piece of excrement—is it a fine dog? The monk said, "If that is so, then [the Buddha's teachings amount to] five thousand and forty..."
"The remaining scrolls would all become superfluous words. The Master said, "I do not know either.
The monk asked, "Since you, Reverend, do not know, why do you tell people not to read or study texts? The Master said, "Once bitten by a snake, one fears even seeing a broken rope.
The Master further cited the case where Chan Master Yan, the founder of the monastery, arrived at Jia Shan. Jia Shan asked him, "Where have you come from? The Master [continued].
Yangshan said, "Cloud-Dwelling Dragon. Yunmen said, "When you came, did the dragon still rise? The Master stepped forward and looked at him with his eyes.
Yangshan said, "To apply more moxa to a burn scar. The Master said, "Why do you, Reverend, afflict yourself so? Yangshan then desisted. The Master commented:
"These two venerable elders, one pressing and one prodding, were like those skilled at wielding the Great Black Sword (Ta'a) who do not injure their own hands."
Nevertheless, there are places reached and places not reached. Entering the hall [for instruction]:
There has never been a mind without an object, nor an object without a mind. To forget both mind and object simultaneously is still not the phrase for arriving home.
When the drum is beaten in Pūrvavideha in the east and Zen is preached in Aparagoyānī in the west, tell me, who is this person?
This is the matter of one's own fundamental nature. A dog licks a hot oil cauldron.
[The Master] ascends the hall and cites Baofu, who, while ill, asked a monk: "I have known you for many years; what famous prescription or wondrous medicine do you have to save me?
The monk replied: "There are indeed many prescriptions. [Baofu continued: "I hear it is said that you, Master, do not know how to observe dietary restrictions. The Master [laughed].
The Master picks up the case and says: This monk is not easy to find. Yet, how could Baofu’s mind truly be satisfied?
At that time, he should have simply said lightly, "How long has the Master been ill? Let us see what kind of words he would have produced.
Had he merely said, "It is unfit for administering medicine," would it not have encompassed both past and present?
On the occasion of the Dragon Boat Festival, he ascended the hall. Master Longya said: "To study the Way, one must first have an awakening;
it is like once having competed in a swift dragon boat race. Though it be an old, empty, and neglected field, only after winning it back once does one finally rest.
Great and small, Longya’s realization of the ground was not yet free; he remained stuck right there. This mountain monk, without sparing a single hair on his brow, shall now clear it away for him.
The Path. Thus one sees that its merit transcends all things and its Way is beyond names and words. It is said: "Delusion and awakening have always been entirely free;
one must row a boat upon level ground. Heaven and earth are vast and undivided, without past or present;
the pure breeze of a thousand years never ceases. Suddenly, someone comes forth and says: "Ruigan is merely nailing down a stake and rocking the oars. A-ha-ha! Take this up!"
Seeing that no one was present, he descended from his seat and ascended the hall. "Today is the fifteenth; the Dharma drum has been struck. A pillar stepped out from the ranks.

As the Elder ascended the seat and then descended, he looked toward his attendant and asked, "What did you just say? The attendant remained silent. Thereupon [the Master] said, "A single character entering the gates of officialdom..."
"Nine oxen could not pull it out.

He ascended the hall. "The wheel of food has not turned for a long time; the steamer is overturned, the kitchen empty, and the hearth cold. The attendant came to announce that he was to ascend the hall.
It causes me to harbor a thousand thoughts and ten thousand reflections; right now, I have no leisure even to endure hunger, much less the time to cast aside three things and let go of two.
In a frantic rush, I don my seven-strip robe, resting my staff across my knees, employing Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra to inspect the myriad phenomena of the universe.
To call this "upwardly sustained" is very much like scratching an itch through a boot. [He descends from his seat.]
Ascending the hall, he said: "A single phrase cuts off the current; ten thousand functions fall silent. Two do not form a pair; one does not form a solitary unit.
He picked up his staff and struck it once: "An iron wall! An iron wall!"
Ascending the hall, he said: "Before the signs of manifestation were distinguished, what a fine news! After the signs of manifestation have been distinguished, the news is entirely absent.
When a single speck of dust enters right concentration, all specks of dust arise as samādhi—like striking a ball upon swift-flowing water."
Ascending the hall, he said: "When meeting, I do not bring it forth; as soon as you raise your intention, you know it exists. My two eyes have been struck out, yet I have left behind a single mouth.
On the summit of a solitary peak, I revile the Buddhas and scold the Patriarchs; the aperture is pierced at the crown of my head.

In the streets of the twelve quarters, I run wild and frantic; a talisman is suspended from my elbow. Changsha’s tiger, Zihu’s dog—pick up this coarse and pungent thorn-brush, and I shall give you a split!"
Ji Lou. Sickness in the Eyes:
Ascending the Hall. For several days, this mountain monk’s sick eyes have been dark and blurred, to the point that east and west could not be distinguished, nor south and north.
Yet, within this state of non-distinction and non-discrimination, there is nonetheless a clarity. A monk asked: "Nine..."
Feng said, "How is it that you hold fast the eye that governs heaven and earth? You are like one who breaks chopsticks to stir the Dragon Gate.

Feng said, "Holding fast is right here; it is like a beggar playing with a rice bowl. The monk asked, "Where is the eye that governs heaven and earth? Feng replied, "A second offense will not be tolerated.

Feng said, "This is precisely the eye that governs heaven and earth; it is like buying high and selling low. The monk asked, "Does it still shed light? Feng said, "What need is there for it to shed light?"

Feng said, "Without borrowing the power of the three luminaries, his tongue drags upon the ground. A monk asked, "If he does not borrow the power of the three luminaries, by what means does he illuminate?
Why is this called the 'Eye of Heaven and Earth'? Feng said, "A dog biting a dry bone. Feng continued, "If it were not thus, one would see ghosts before one's own skull;
that is truly the talk of one who sees ghosts. Jiu-feng’s long blowing and slow striking was what he himself called his own skillful means.

How formidable! Yet, alas, this monk has long frequented the halls of practice; his exchanges of verse have been flawless. Even those with the "eye that grasps heaven and earth" have not yet seen through him.
Today, it is not that I am encroaching upon his domain or seizing his market share; rather, it is because having suffered much illness myself, I am well-acquainted with the nature of medicines.
Do you wish to recognize the eye that holds fast to heaven and earth? (He strikes the meditation staff. When the light of dawn has not yet parted, all gaze;
yet once daybreak comes, it is merely ordinary.
To the assembly: Ruiyan has a single pivot; though extremely small, it pervades the universe. It does not abide before the time of Vimalacitra, nor does it fall within the realm of the Lumen.
Later, rising at dawn, I encountered a darkening sky; sleeping at night, I met the daylight of day. The orphaned child has a lifespan of a thousand springs;

with white hair, he has barely emerged from infancy. *Param*. Entering the hall: Outside the eaves, the rain falls through the night; every sound belongs entirely to him. Clearly and repeatedly pointed out and annotated—what more need be said?
Hesitation. Upon receiving the bamboo whisk bestowed by the Venerable Master Mingqing Yingzhong, he ascended the hall, held it up, and showed it to the assembly, saying:
"Its vigorous nodes pierce the clouds; its solitary standard defies the snow. Its roots were established before the beginningless kalpas; its substance was conceived beyond the Three Vehicles. One...
The sword is split in two without the need for deliberation; grasped with a confident hand, it causes gods to cry out and ghosts to weep.
It is not something a fly-whisk can equal, nor can it be compared to a tortoise’s hair. Where it strikes, thunder crashes through the hibernating chambers;

when held upright, the blade leans against the vast sky. Master Ma folds his hands in surrender; Baizhang bows his head in submission at the mere sight of it. Such is its wondrous function. There is...
"Regarding such supernatural powers as these, do you all know their place of origin? If you do not yet know, go ask Master Mingqing.
Having said this, he struck the meditation seat and descended from it.

Ascending the hall on the occasion of the Green Sprouts ceremony: "To explain the meaning by relying on the sutras is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods; to depart from even a single word of the sutras is to speak like a demon.

For days on end, we have gathered the assembly in the mountains to read the sutras, merely to ensure the protection of the grain sprouts. We see only that the white surface is paper and the black marks are characters.
Since we neither establish our own position apart from the sutras nor explain their meaning by relying on them, tell me: is this the Buddha’s teaching? Or is it...?
Moshan said, "Ha! He then ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "What is the phrase that encompasses heaven and earth? The Master said, "A live sparrow in the mouth of a fierce tiger.
The monk asked, "What is the phrase that cuts off all streams? The Master said, "An eight-sided staff in the hand of Vajrapāṇi."
The monk asked, "What is the phrase of 'following the waves and chasing the currents'? The Master said, "Li Bai grasping the moon; Zhang Qian riding the raft.
The Master then said, "Seeing with eyes as if blind; speaking with a mouth as if mute. Solely honored within the three realms, above heaven and below earth.
To gather it up and let it go; the cast-iron hammer has been eaten by worms. Whether there is profit or loss, one does not leave the marketplace. Three.
Furthermore, singing a "Ba" song under the moon, he inadvertently startled the King of Brahma from his sleep.
Entering the hall, he held up his staff and said, "This is Deshan’s staff. He struck the ground with the staff and said, "This is Linji’s shout.
"You all must take care not to mistake error for truth! Have you not seen what Master Xuansha said?
It is just like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night;
it is never diminished by being struck, nor does it scatter when it encounters waves. Yet, this is still a matter belonging to the shore of birth and death.

There are those who, upon hearing such a teaching, immediately begin to deliberate on the east and calculate on the west, seeking elsewhere for a way to escape. They do not realize that the cow-pen and the horse-stable are already perfectly complete.
The Jue Monastery, the mountain of fire and blades, and the realm of cool serenity—when one reaches this place, skill is exhausted and only clumsiness remains;
one can do nothing but follow the wind to turn the rudder and drift with the waves. Nevertheless, unless one is a true connoisseur, it is all in vain to speak of enduring the cold of winter.

Ascending the hall: This morning is the first day of the seventh month; the autumn wind stirs at the corner of the eaves. The unsurpassed gate of liberation is wide open, without obstruction or confinement.
Whether coming from the east or the west, from the south or the north, beneath this bright window they are arranged according to the Dharma.
Whether Buddha or Patriarch, whether sage or ordinary person, they are all given a send-off upon the palm of the hand. With host and guest, with total embodiment and total function.

A wind of refined elegance that penetrates to the very marrow; the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. The ocean of three thousand lands is deep and silent; Mount Sumeru rises solitary and towering on its own.

At the small *prātimokṣa* ceremony marking the end of the summer retreat: the period of *vassa* is complete. In a single thought, ten thousand years pass; the sack is opened, and everything is settled—a hundred matters resolved, a thousand tasks accomplished.

Whether south of heaven or north of earth, there is nothing that is not the wondrous field of Perfect Enlightenment (*yuanjue*). Whether east of the stream or west of the stream, it is all the king’s water and grass.
In this way and that way, one clears a patch of fallow land and sows a basketful of millet.

Not in this way and not in that way, one eats a single meal at midday and sleeps a single sleep after nightfall. In this way and not in this way, not in this way yet in this way—one brings forth the leaning staff.
A celestial long sword cuts through the entanglements of the *lùbù* (military dispatch). Directly, there is nothing above to grasp or look up to; below, one’s own self is severed.
Constant radiance manifests before one, standing like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high. At this very moment, do you all understand this news?
If you do not yet know it, you cannot avoid casting sand and scattering earth upon the pure ground. Worldly...
When the Honored One was first born, he pointed one hand toward heaven and one hand toward earth, walked seven steps around, and gazed in the four directions, saying:
"In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the Honored One. Is this not that very message?

Whether it be the Seven and the Four of the Western Heaven, or the Two and the Three of this Eastern Land—whether they employ the staff, the shout, roll the ball before the hall, or act within the room—it is all this.

"Peaceful waters"—is this not that very message? As for the rest—the "three pounds of flax," the "dry dung pellet," the "cypress tree in the courtyard," the "donkey eating grass in the back garden," the story of Zhaozhou examining the old woman, and the story of Baizhang and the wild ducks—though they may appear three-faced or two-sided, or differ in ten thousand ways and a thousand variations, are they not all, without exception, this very same message? To engage in such theoretical discussion... [is to look down...]
To follow such expedient means before those with clear eyes—what kind of drowsy talk is this? Have you not heard it said: "The one path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages;
students weary their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections"? [He suddenly seizes his staff, strikes once, and says:
"All shattered! No old nest or trap! Having grasped the nostrils, he has lost his mouth. If you wish to hide your body within the Northern Dipper, you must..."
After joining his palms toward the Southern Dipper, he spoke again in verse: "When summer ends and you roll up your mat, where will you go?
I urge you to temporarily rest this mind for now. The furnaces of all quarters have grown cold as ash; The gate of Shaoshi is as deep as the sea.

If you wish to awaken and surpass the Buddhas and Patriarchs, Do not take intellectual understanding to be your inner core. By the Stone of Awakened Clarity, one may find delight; Together let us listen..."
The pines and winds perform the true sound.
[The Master] ascends the hall: "In summer there is the untying of knots; the Dharma has no fixed characteristics. The meaning of existence and non-existence is like a bubble-flower in the sky.

South of the Celestial Terrace and North of the Five Terraces—these are at the soles of everyone's feet. Whether you step upon them or not, I shall set them aside and say no more. [He then stepped forward.]
If Cheng Hu should ask where you have come from, by all means do not say you have come from Ruiyan; let him doubt for thirty years. Ascending the hall, [the Master said]:

"When the Dharma-vehicle is proclaimed once, the Tripitaka is rendered inexpressible. When the Patriarchal command is fully upheld, heaven and earth lose their luster. Like a king’s precious sword, its divine majesty is chilling;
should one wish to charge forward, one would find corpses strewn about with bare bones. To proceed exclusively in this manner is to cut off the Way."

The people are scattered; deliberating in a secret chamber, there is no further connection to be made. He picks up his staff and says: "Last night, the western wind brought autumn to the pillows and mats;
countless cicadas clamor in the high trees."
Ascending the hall: Ten thousand miles without a cloud, yet the blue sky remains; a thousand waves rise in competition, yet the volume of water suffers no loss.
Movement and stillness are difficult to encompass; light and dark find no foothold. You monks, walking alone and standing solitary—this is already a burden too heavy to bear.
Furthermore, if one acts otherwise, it is like a moth rushing into a flame.
The Master asked a monk, "Yesterday was sunny, today it rains. What is the true suchness of this single essence? The monk replied, "Whom are you asking, Preceptor?
The Master said, "I am asking you, the Venerable One, right now. The monk said, "I understood it just a moment ago, but now I do not."
[The Master] said, "Understood. He then struck [the assembly] twice with his palms and asked, "Tell me, was this a reward for him, or was it a punishment?

Indeed, after three years had passed since Deshan’s passing, they took that very level ground and dug a pit therein.
Yunmen addressed the assembly, saying:
"The world is this vast, yet the stone woman cuts rabbit horns from her waist; on the back of the iron ox, one scrapes tortoise hair.
Although these are merely ordinary matters, for a thousand ages he surpasses others in his skillful means."

When Deshan entered the gate, he struck him down with a staff after staff to transmit the mind-seal; the entire universe ceased its practice. The Abbot of Gaomao Village had once been a disciple of Longtan.
Baizhang’s Wild Fox:
When spring arrives in the gardens, one is moved by the sights and sounds; before the window, a single bird sings in a hundred ways.
It is only because of the passage of impermanence that the name "Back-Tongued" has endured through the ages, impossible to erase.
The fish leaps;
its head moves, its tail moves—vividly alive and agile. The vast net and great mesh cannot restrain it. With a single bound it soars, passing through the Celestial Gate;
the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea is startled and sticks out his tongue.

When Gānzhì prepared the congee, he did so with a mind set on serving the congee; where was there any contradiction? When the attendant went out the door, Nánquán smashed the cauldron—this is the talk of the bamboo staff.
He raises the bamboo whisk. The sun shines and heaven is present before one. Attempting to distinguish between "with" and "against," it is like searching for a needle in the great ocean.
The master calls out, "Master! again and again; those who practice fear falling into emptiness. Jushi only raised his finger; Shigong only drew his bow.

Xinghua’s striking of his fellow practitioner was the true command being put into practice. Even if a Buddha were to come, he would strike; his mouth was like a blood-basin, leaving no room for explanation.
Xinghua struck Kebin.
Raising a child, one fears most being stroked like a cat's fur. The tradition of Xinghua’s house is contrary to the world:
he was bound with a staff and fined, then driven out of the monastery, so that he might establish his own livelihood with empty hands.
I have heard that Donglang shouted "Ho!
while Bimo held up his staff to catch a mouse; Ziming posted a notice and drew ghostly talismans.
How can these compare to the elegance of Old Xinghua, who scattered real pearls within the purple silk curtains?

Entering directly with a single blade, sitting upright facing the eaves to test a master of the Way—yet even such direct entry remains fraught with error. A shout bursts forth like the moon over a thousand crags;
alas, how can one avoid falling entirely into a thicket of weeds?

When brought forth, it serves as a single pair of unperforated iron hammers for people; among them, one is the heaviest. Even if someone could discern and distinguish it, it would still be like ghosts contending over a lacquered bucket.

Yin-feng lifted his water pitcher and poured its contents directly in front of him; he was always adept at seeking advantage for himself. Wearing only his undergarments and single robe, he once startled the assembly;
with a single blow, he struck within the hall of San-sheng.
Shitou said: "So it is, yet it is also so.
The vast ocean is already boundless—what need is there to dredge it? Mount Tai is already towering—there is no need to bolster it. A single ancient road is as straight as a bowstring;
clap your hands, sing aloud, and go home."
The Three Sages ask of Xuefeng:
Meeting suddenly and unexpectedly, their smiling faces unfold; together they take each other’s hands and ascend the high platform.
But when the conversation reaches the point of paradox, angry words and wrathful fists strike the face.
The landscape of Jia Shan features emerald cliffs and azure peaks, steep and profound; flowers bloom and leaves fall from antiquity to the present.
Jia Shan turns the rudder with the wind; Fayan slices open the belly and gouges out the heart. *Oṃ bulin*. *Oṃ chilin*.
The eaves-boards of Han have never drunk water, yet they know the source; their nostrils are clearly missing half.
Having stripped off the flesh-grabbing undershirt, they are summoned back to be lashed once more with a heavy whip.
A single breath turns the entire Great Canon;
Muzhou has a mouth but no tongue. Profound meanings layer upon layer, yet all are encompassed in a single phrase. To report this to the Chan travelers of the Five Lakes:
do not casually act like a duck startled by thunder.
When the two Hall Heads let out a shout, the two halls shout together;
each exerts their own majestic authority. Who says that the place of accomplishment lies within the domain of Linji?
Puhua shook his bell amidst the clamor of the marketplace, revealing the Great Function within the dust of the world; this was not like idly drumming upon lips of leather.
The sound of the clapper shook the three thousandfold world-system, while oysters, clams, and snails slept in utter delusion.
Mingzhao says: "The weather is cold. Ascending the hall, he said:
"Though the wind-swept heights and the warm chamber are distinct, establishing one's destiny and settling one's body are in every way the same.
The lion cub roars spontaneously; how could Mingzhao be intentionally deceiving you?"
Baoshou opens the hall and fully upholds the true command; sun and moon grow dim. East, west, south, and north, all vie to hasten toward it. Baizhang sees wild ducks while wandering the mountains;
Daowu’s response to the question captures the essential loincloth.
The ancients did not attend the hall;
the flavor of the oil-cakes on the altar was truly distinct. Indeed, they ate until they were most exceptionally full.
How pitiable are the shameless attendants, who bow their heads in greeting and request them to attend the hall.
Felling the central tree of the grove;
tearing up the ancestral covenant; a heroic spirit that would have surpassed that of Xiang Yu; yet so poor as to lack even a nail for a workbench.
The bride rides the donkey while her mother-in-law leads;
once she is seated securely upon the beast, today she joyfully enters the gate. Having met her husband, the "檀郎" (Tánláng), her innermost thoughts are now fit to be discussed.

Wujou asked: "The two elders Xuan and Shao snatched food from the mouth of a fierce tiger and probed for pearls beneath the chin of a black dragon. Had they not possessed such innate strategic skill, their scalps would surely have been severed."
“Dry dung-spoon,” said Yunmen;
“dry dung-spoon. It scorches the earth and smokes the heavens. Everyone together clears it away and sends it off upon the ferryboat at the riverhead.
Sumeru Mountain.
Mount Sumeru rises abruptly, leaning against the azure sky; it thrusts out the eyes of the *jiaoming* insect with lightning speed.
Were one to personally reach its summit in a single day, only then would one know that it is not the same as the other mountains.
The saw cuts the scale-beam;
picking up the scale-beam, he uses it to cut the saw. The lantern and the pillar clamor and chatter.
Among them, those who have not yet forgotten their attachments continue to deliberate upon this marvel without ceasing.
When coming from the four quarters and eight directions, how can one hide?
An ancient temple is filled with anxiety; ghostly faces and divine heads appear everywhere before one.
When one waits for the wind and rain to pass, the bright sun shines as ever in the midst of heaven.
At Wangzhou Pavilion, I have already met you;

the Master has been meeting you for a long time. Why is your head-skin still so stubborn? Though the foul water was ladled out and splashed upon you three times, it remains as if we were face-to-face yet separated by a thousand mountains.
Jiashan addressed the assembly: "Before one's eyes there is no dharma;
to set it forth on a platter is still hesitant. Hidden away within a covering bag, how could it be known? In the end, there are thorns within the mire;
one does not know when one has stepped upon them."
National Teacher Wuye says:
"A single red thread pulls at both ends. How can this story be brought to completion within the monastic community?
I would rather decisively snap it all apart for him—swinging on a swing upon the back of empty space.
Lingyun saw the peach blossoms;
Lingyun saw the peach blossoms. Slanting branches, rows of budding twigs. Blooming once every year, they are as profuse as crimson clouds.
Xuan Sha said: "How perfectly true! How perfectly true!"

I dare say my elder brother has not yet attained thorough penetration. Behind his back he secretly clenches his fists; though he may break through the Ghost Gate Barrier, when drinking water one must guard against choking.
His words do not unfold the matter, for they have seized the throat and pierced the nostrils. From the Eastern Land to the Western Heaven, the head is light while the tail is heavy.
Juding asked about those two from Langya:
one who pursued the Way until he reached the heavens, and one who remained stubbornly wild to the very end. To each I give thirty harsh pears.
Now, return to me and observe the etiquette between host and guest.

In speech or silence, one traverses the realms of transcendence and subtlety; a clever housewife can bake a cake without flour. A simpleton may purchase a village for all his wealth, yet the mandate over Wu and Yue is a merit that cannot be shared.
Do not let the iron covenant burden your descendants.
Zhaozhou visited Daowu;
his leopard-skin loincloth was mottled and variegated. Wearing it out before others, he startled all who saw or heard him.
Had Zhaozhou not been familiar with it from long ago, this scene of terror would be beyond description.

Linji’s passing away was a "white-thief" maneuver beyond compare; his face-to-face deception cannot be discussed. He took the property of the ten directions’ monastic community and, at the time of his departure, entrusted it to his descendants.
A monk asked: "Qianfeng’s smoke-pipe and Yanqu’s rain-cloak—monks wander with their bowls in the wild; wherever they go, there is nothing that does not obscure their own numinous spirit.
It is truly lamentable that these two venerable elders, despite their advanced age, still present a lacquer bucket to others."

Awakening to the Way upon hearing a sound—form and sound are mounted together; do not seek outside. Striking the east sets the west in motion. The red flowers and green willows are but momentary affairs;
the barking dog and braying donkey never cease.
Grand Master Lu Xing asked Nanquan about the "single branch of flowers.
Nanquan pointed it out, saying: "It is as poisonous as the 'tortoise-nose snake' of the Southern Mountains. No one in the world knows how to handle it;
it is most worthy of praise, yet not worthy of praise."
Yunmen took up his staff and cited a teaching that says:
"The spring colors have no high or low; the flower branches are naturally long or short. Though the Taihang Mountains are perilous paths, people continue to travel them as before."
Xuan Sha’s Three Kinds of Illness:
Xuan Sha did not leave Feiyuan Ridge; he stirred up the monastic community with myriad complications.
Even this does not constitute a true hero—Lingyun was still deceived by him.

When Xuansha saw a newly arrived monk, he never hesitated to reveal [the truth]; first, he struck him with a fist to the chest. His words distinguished the pure from the impure; yet even so, one would still fall into the fetters of conceptualization.
Upon this bare lump of flesh—
A mass of raw flesh, scorched by the sun and buffeted by the wind; through spiritual powers it manifests in hundreds of thousands of ways. All at once it is cast away before people;
beat the drum and let everyone come to see.
Baizhang attended Mazu while they traveled through the mountains;

upon returning, he wept for Li Ling and Su Wu at the parting at He-liang. Those who remained were sorrowful, while those who traveled were joyful. Let us cease debating right and wrong throughout past and present:
the lands of Han and the heavens of Hu share but one bright moon.
Yangqi asked a monk: "How do you swallow the brambles?
The fierce flames of the red furnace reach to the heavens; the sun and moon withdraw their chariots and Chang'e weeps. Iron walls and silver mountains rise ten thousand fathoms high;
reaching this point, they too must be melted into liquid."
The Three-Legged Donkey:

Yangqi rides backward upon a three-legged donkey; the Elder of Hunan follows close behind. Passing through cities and over mounds like a flash of lightning, the weary, slow-paced steed can only sigh in exhaustion.
The price of rice in Luling is the very meaning of Qingyuan; it is easy to see but difficult to recognize. Soft as a ball of cotton, hard as a whetstone.
The door-bolt of the Great Being, the ruler and compass of Master Baofu. If you ask further how it is, who would you have take the staff?
In the back garden, the donkey eats grass; once full, all are satisfied. This is not like the starving Han-lu, who vainly gnaws on dry bones.
A small fish swallows a large fish; a red banner is planted upon the water. I wish to speak, but words fail me; beneath the trees, contemplate well.
The five heinous crimes have heard the thunder;
last night the iron ox broke its horns. It has smashed through empty space with a *pò-pò* roar. This morning, the traces and origins are suddenly clarified:
it was none other than Li Babai from the eastern village.
The mouth is the gate of calamity;
one word, when applied with immediacy, cuts off all comparison. The five lakes and four seas boil like hot soup. Upon the tip of a snail’s horn, heaven and earth are vast;
within the flash of a stone-fire, the sun and moon endure long.
The Song of the Twelve Hours at Longmen:
Hour after hour, day after day; day after day, hour after hour—continuous and dense, strange and marvelous.
Chanting praises atop the bell tower.
Severing both ends, one strikes at the center; this stirs up disputes that the waters of the sea cannot wash away. Venerable Siṃha, once the flowing water has passed, it does not return;
once the petals have fallen, they are hard to place back upon the branch. At the end of the night beneath a solitary candle, the mind’s threads are as tangled as silk.
Bajiao addressed the assembly:
"Alas! You wandering monk, when have you ever let go of your staff? Seize it and break it into two pieces!
(Please provide the final line.)
The ten knowledges share the same truth;
twelve street corners have guest toilets installed. Do not allow people to come and defecate recklessly.
No matter how skillfully you might dig a well with a single spade, when you lift your eyes, the hawk has already flown to Silla.

Having swallowed the waters of the West River in a single draught and picked up a single black pearl, he claimed it was beyond price in the human world; yet upon encountering the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea,
he regarded it as mere refuse.
Yunmen’s Mirror:
Yunmen’s single mirror reflects ten thousand sufferings and a thousand sorrows; the devas cease their music, and Śakra shakes his head.
*Ei!* The spring wind that causes such turmoil will never truly rest.
The Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū carves a boat to seek a lost sword, expending his efforts in vain; he waits by a stump for a rabbit, yet it shall not come.
The wren merely clings to the branches of the mugwort, while the great garuḍa bird spreads its wings to soar upon the wind.
As for those who bestow [offerings] upon you, they do not call them fields of merit.
A white-nosed Kunlun dances the Zhezhi; when the spring wind blows through the courtyard and the flowers fall, thousands of villages and ten thousand hamlets vie to gaze upon him.
Which of these people originally lacks eyebrows above their eyes?
Abiding at all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts.

Whether opening the sitting mat and spreading the alms bowl, or picking up the spoon and setting down the chopsticks—each and every action is already manifest and complete. What need is there for inscriptions on stone monuments?
At the very moment of seeing, that which sees is not itself the seeing.
A barren woman carries a basket, empty-handed and barefoot; she searches for crabs upon the mountain of yellow reeds.
The mountain streams and peaks wind and turn deeper and deeper, until not a single person is encountered.
The practitioner of purity does not enter nirvana;
the sun does not require fire to be hot, nor does the moon require wind to be cool. Wherever one may be, amidst green mountains and clear waters, I sit upon Mount Dongting by the Xiang River.
The five dharmas, the three natures, the two kinds of selflessness, and the ten [categories] have originally been five pairs. Old Śākyamuni’s face is yellow; few people walk upon the crystal palace.
Dogs bark and donkeys bray throughout the Great Tang.

To save from the perils of childbirth, the donor family prays for deliverance from such hardships; in a single word, they find accord in an instant. This is my own good son, whom no beating could kill;
it is difficult to trust another’s horse and seek to ride it.
In the year Wushen of the Zhizheng era, I took refuge with Master Bao of Nangu Valley on Mount Yongle while fleeing the chaos of war.
Master Bao’s grandson, Preceptor Xiong of Gushan, remarked: "In the past, Dahui of Zhushan also lived at Yunmen Hermitage to escape the turmoil of war."
There are one hundred and ten ancient cases of composed verses (*gāthās*). Now that this Master has arrived, his traces happen to be similar to theirs.
Moreover, as the Gate of the School (*zongmen*) has fallen into desolation, the Master ought to continue its lingering resonance.
Without considering my own unworthiness, I have ventured to compose these coarse words, equal in number [to the original], to respond to the Master’s inquiry. This is the recognition of Wu Cun.
Zhaozhou visits the Upper and Lower Hermitages:
An old fisherman with white hair sits in his fishing boat. Reeds line both banks; it is the same autumn everywhere. The silvery scales do not bite; the river wind is cold.
He gathers in his line and returns home to rest.
When Bodhidharma saw Emperor Wu, the jade halls and pearl towers were all wide open; alone and humble, he presented the ten-thousand-year cup.
Though he did not receive the sovereign’s favor, he returned with the celestial fragrance still filling his sleeves.

The cypress tree in front of the courtyard—only at eighty years of age did he begin his pilgrimage. Every strand of hair has reached its root in whiteness; feigning deafness and pretending to be mute, he seeks advantage.
When asked about the West, he answers with the courtyard cypress.
De Shan saw Longtan:
his head and horns loom large as he lies within the azure pool; from the four mountains, only rising green mists are seen. Sometimes when touched, wind and thunder stir;
amidst the great flood, Mount Sumeru reveals but a single hairpin.
Huangbo ascended the hall. As soon as the assembly had gathered, he drove them all away at once with his staff.
He then called out, "Assembly! Assembly! When the assembly turned their heads, Huangbo said: "The moon is like a drawn bow; little rain, much wind.

A thousand-fathom formidable pass, cut off from its neighbors, Where passage to and fro is impossible—steep and jagged. How pitiable are those in the north and south who greedily pursue their journey!"
The wind and rain were piercing and chilling, enough to kill one with sorrow.

Ciming posted a proclamation—a divine edict emerging from the forbidden city. Thousands of gates and ten thousands of households were all struck with doubt and alarm. As soon as they heard the messenger’s announcement...
Afterwards, they bowed their heads to the ground and shouted "Mount!
to celebrate the Great Peace.

Regarding the minor funeral rites, West Hall Master Cong raised the catafalque. I am one who has cast away cleverness and intelligence, extinguished all knowledge and views, and is a man who fears neither birth nor death. Adieu!
Xiazhu held his mountain-axe; it was precisely a matter of going east or west.
Nan Chu of Jing Mountain served tea; Pang Gong lifted his sack; Yangshan shook the tree.

These two great elders each displayed their banners and spears, acting with mastery over both killing and giving life. Yet, when they come before our Head Teacher, they are of no use at all. Why is this?
The Dragon Gate rises ten thousand fathoms; even birds cannot fly across it.
To arrive there for a moment and behold the Elder rising from his shrine, one must utterly forget all views if the Great Function is to manifest before them.
When all views are exhausted, birth and death are immediately empty. The home and the road are not separate things at all. Let the light burst forth from the crown of the head!
Tianhu said, "Nai, the head monk, is enduring the fire. This evening sermon by Ciming is a performance of death. He has raised the fire-cloud;
the flames reach Mount Kunlun, where jade and stone are burned together. Only true gold can withstand such smelting."
He received the fire of the monastery head; he received and endured harsh blows and kicks, whereupon he understood how to transcend life and death.
The oil lamp, leaking and shaking the earth, emitted light; the vajra-ring was not worth a single coin. Amidst a mass of blazing flames, he set up his fishing line and caught a carp one foot long.
The Sealed Treasury-Master rises from his shrine; the Seal of Vairocana is brilliantly radiant. Those who do not know how to employ it will inevitably encounter obstructions.
On level ground, there are countless dead; one who penetrates the thicket of thorns is a true adept.
"Puweinuo Fire! At the eastern edge of Fucheng, it was no different than it is today.

Why did you only exhaust your cleverness and extinguish your active delusions by heading toward the spot where a wooden barrel hoop exploded? Holding up a torch, he said: 'Light this fire and look; how thick is that face-skin?'"
The Administrative Head (Yun) locked the coffin; the spiritual mechanism moved secretly, and the mirror of wisdom shone forth, until the three-legged donkey leaped and galloped away.
Treading through the void—what use is this very lock? Monk Sheng raises the coffin;
he snaps the holy arrow. What a world of peace! Birth, old age, sickness, and death.

"From where have you come? Let go and he falls; support him and he rises. Like shooting stars and flashing lightning across three thousand li, the Chief Administrator of the Monastery (Changdu Si) has raised the reliquary shrine.
He cherished the monastery’s property as if protecting his own eyes, yet in a single thought, he has cast it all down with total detachment.
Do not linger upon the Terrace of Nirvana; at the head of the 'Victorious Gate' (Shenghuo Men), you must advance further still."
Shengdui held up a firebrand. Yangqi looked at Baiyun and burst into laughter. "This is very much like forcing a live snake to transform into a dragon;
it is entirely a gate of death, neither of which is a path of life. He threw down the firebrand and said, "I call this fire, but you must not call it fire."
Elder Qi said: "Before the Buddha was born and before he attained full realization, there was a singular, extraordinary matter.
It encompasses the cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, yet it cannot be grasped by others. It cannot be captured by thought or mental speculation.
Only when you realize it directly will you know that throughout immeasurable kalpas, taking on body after body has been like fire burning ice."
The Han Chief Administrator raises the coffin. This morning, a troop of dead men escort a living man. He has passed through the Diamond Circle and swallowed the thorny jujube fruit.
Throughout the ten directions of the world, there is not a whisper of news. Nevertheless, it is like dropping a medicine bag behind a funeral carriage.

There is one who oversees the fire: he sets aside the leaking oil lamp and releases the originally possessed spiritual light, which pierces through the night of the dark alleys of birth and death throughout kalpas.
The moon does not wait for the wind to be cool; the sun does not wait for fire to be hot.

The Way-purifier raises the shrine; reaching the profound and vast Way, its propagation depends on the person. At midnight at Huangmei, the robe was transmitted—this greatly resembles playing with a false image as if it were real.
When the Real does not stand, the False is fundamentally empty; a dead snake leaps out from the grass, knocking down the peak of Mount Sumeru.
Man Shuji has filled his records with *gūchā* (bone tea); he is full to the brim with literary compositions and carries wooden plaques across his entire body.

Yet, when it comes to being called upon for a direct encounter, he is truly nothing but skin and bone. Had Nan Piantou not been struck by Ciming’s merciless, lethal blow, he would have inevitably been drowned in the stagnant water of Lestam.
When a man is at a painted pavilion buying wine, he invites others to come and eat at Zhaozhou’s.
Cha Cheng:

Senior Monk Cheng opened the coffin and displayed Master Cheng’s meditation seat; there was no need for hesitation. Fufeng: While Senior Monk Fu was in Yangzhou, he attained immediate enlightenment upon hearing the painted horn.
Gaoting: Seeing Deshan from across the river, he simply strode straight toward him. On the road, he encountered a dead man.
Do not strike and kill the snake; take it home in a bottomless basket.
When Mingdu Guan enters the stupa, he clearly knows it is this very thing, yet he cannot open his mouth to speak. When he clearly knows it is not this very thing, he can open his mouth and speak.
Having cut off both barriers, his natural wind-bone is revealed; he hits the mark every time, a hundred times out of a hundred.

The holy arrow has left the bowstring; it has pierced through in every direction. From south of the Xiang River to north of the Tan Lake, how many times have I descended for you into the Azure Dragon’s lair?
Monk Yidu, though you have emerged from the dust, you do not understand ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); this is because your emotional attachments (*kleśa*) have not been severed.

Though you are advanced in years, you have not realized the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*); this is because the Great Matter remains unresolved. Right now, the four elements have already separated; cut them off decisively where they have not yet been severed.
Not yet fully understood, Yangqi’s carrying-pole is twisted into firewood and burned; amidst the mass of blazing flames, snow and hail fly crosswise.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shunzhong*, Volume Three;
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shunzhong*, Volume Four.
Compiled by the Dharma-heir junior disciple Bhikṣu Jūtei and others,
*Praise for Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva*, edited at Cuishan Chan Temple.
The Abbot of Puzhao Chan Monastery in Zhenjiang Prefecture, Fazu Wenhui, purchased a hanging scroll depicting the Bodhisattva.
His compassionate countenance was most majestic and grand. Wu Cun reverently burned incense and offered this praise: [The text continues with the eulogy.]
I prostrate to the Great Compassionate Father who pities the world. Through hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization, he has attained nirvana;

yet within that nirvana, he dwells nowhere. Therefore, he is able to manifest thirty-two transformation bodies. Since the karmic fruits experienced by sentient beings differ, it would be difficult to transform them if he did not appear in their own likeness.
Thus, our Bodhisattva carefully discerns what is appropriate, responding universally according to conditions to perform Buddha-work. Regarding the two natures of sense organs and objects—
Consciousness is the sovereign. Within that which manifests from consciousness, there is no limit. From this, the six classes of ordinary beings and the four types of noble ones emerge;
therefore, it is named the Tathāgatagarbha. When the nature of consciousness turns back, the original truth is revealed, and the gateway of perfect penetration opens its lock and key.

All who come according to their direction are able to enter, like a child approaching its father without any doubt. The sentient beings of this Sahā world are deluded regarding their fundamental hearing; they follow...
Sounds flow and circulate, leading one into false views; like a mountain pheasant that treasures its plumage, it gazes at its reflection by the stream and dies without regret.
The Bodhisattva exerts the power of diligence to skillfully guide others to the stage of True Suchness (Tathatā). Ultimately, all is clearly understood to be like a dream or an illusion;
hearing and the nature of hearing are both perfectly interfused. I vow that all sentient beings in the world shall resolve their wills to practice together and attain this realization.
Eternally abiding, the realm of perfect penetration brings all categories of beings back to their source. He who opens this essential path—if it were not for a Sage, who else could do so?

It is only our Great Being, who gives rise to kindness and exercises compassion, entering the ocean of existence to serve as our staff and our refuge. I now take refuge in him, never wavering in thought after thought.

The thoughts of the Great Being likewise attend to me; his mindfulness and my mindfulness are neither identical nor separate, like a great round mirror or a wish-fulfilling gem, its divine radiance profound and serene, its function unimpaired. May all sentient beings cast out lust, anger, and delusion.
Equally contemplating arising and ceasing, one realizes this *tathatā*.
Practicing profound *prajñā*, form and emptiness are non-dual, like an illusory vajra. The body and mind are reduced to ashes; yet, upon hearing a cry, one comes to rescue those in suffering.

Without falling away from great compassion, one unites with the mundane while merging with the ultimate truth; without relying on sacred wisdom, one attains the perfect realization through the single gateway of the ear-faculty, thereby harmonizing with the supreme fruit of all Buddhas of the ten directions—how could this be grasped by the mind or expressed in words, or even be subject to conceptual thought?

Azure cliffs lean against the heavens, revealing the phrase of the precipice; the bright moon rests upon the water, manifesting the true body. Mind and phenomena are perfectly interfused, utterly transcending the sense bases and their objects.
How can what is seen with the eyes compare to what is heard directly by the ears?
To preach the Dharma with the mouth, the mouth must eventually cease; to preach the Dharma with the body, the body must eventually perish.
Only our Great Being sits serenely within the moon reflected in water; in every land and every atom, he preaches without speaking.
With his left hand supporting his chin and his right hand resting upon his knee, what he had preached was forgotten; all became profoundly still and empty.
It was like seasonal rain that nourishes and causes all things to grow: once the rain has ceased its work, the things themselves have nothing to claim as their own gain.
If one shows a fish to people, they pay it no mind; if one shows them a pearl, they consider it extraordinary.
To seek to control the human heart, one might drape a string of pearls upon the ground, yet nothing can be gained thereby. This is the true prediction of enlightenment.
His manifestations are boundless; how could there ever be intentional action? He is tranquil and unmoving, yet from the beginning he has never ceased his non-action.

He reveals the realm of inconceivable liberation and gathers the true refuge of purity amidst the five turbidities. His noble stages are non-regressive, and the flames of his wisdom shine forever long.
He topples the precipice and lets forth a great roar; the toad swallows the jade hare of the moon.
Sound is the voice of the Buddha; form is the form of the Buddha. Dissolving the dust of defilement and revolving toward luminosity, one realizes entry therein at every place.
I bow my head to the Great Being who serves as a model for all beings; may all sentient beings universally attain the power of fearlessness.
Swift cascades and startling thunder; tall pines lean like parasols. Amidst both clamor and silence lies the Vajra Samādhi.

By turning the hearing back upon itself until hearing is exhausted, one transcends the subtle and the minute; at the gateway of the six senses, the mechanism of the mind naturally ceases. The youth does not come, and spring is desolate;
by the precious vase, the willows sway in gentle dependence.
Sitting upright upon the seat of the Dharma-emptiness, his manifested bodies pervade the dust motes of all lands. Amidst boundless sounds and forms, he alone reveals the person of original nature.

Within a single hair-tip lies the realm of the Universal Gate; at the tips of a hundred blades of grass resides the body of sovereign freedom. The pearl from the dragon’s jaw is naturally free of blemish;
the bright mirror upon its stand is fundamentally without dust.
Praise for Guanyin Carrying a Fish Basket:

The glistening scales within the basket are fresh and lively, truly enviable. Had she not encountered one who understands her trade, who would have cast even a glance upon them? Held aloft in her bare hands, she moves through the bustling market;
atop her head, the golden sun flies as swift as an arrow.
Clearly there are live fish in the basket; every cry announces it to all who know. Such a fine transaction goes unrecognized by anyone.
When will you let go of body and mind?
What a fine scaled fish—who would be willing to buy it? With hands grasping and releasing, one still hesitates and lingers. One cannot say that sentient beings lack the seeds of awakening;
yet how can they help it, for the ocean of karmic retribution is vast and deep?
Praise for Avalokiteśvara Walking the Path:

No one greets him from before, nor does anyone follow behind. He holds a round bead in his hand, his steps measured and slow. He turns his head to see that the dust of worldly toil is as deep as the sea;
when will he have delivered all sentient beings?
The Venerable Miaozhan’s Inscription on the Pumenpin (Universal Gate Chapter) Eulogy for the Avalokiteśvara Image:
The Thirty-two Responsive Bodies. Nowhere is there dwelling or attachment; lifting up a single tip of a hair, how vast and expansive is the Universal Gate!
The Wondrous, Profound, and All-Holding Lord of Immovability unties the bonds of affliction for all sentient beings.
The Venerable Lín of Cuìyán has inscribed this eulogy for the Lotus Sūtra Stūpa:
"Only this precious stūpa constantly manifests in the world; it is neither chosen nor subject to change. It stands firm like a lofty mountain, where not even a speck of dust can settle."
Profoundly serene and pure, its dimensions are perfectly proportioned; it responds universally to all heights and depths, pervading the entire realm of *sāhasra* worlds.

It radiates great light that shatters the prisons of delusion and opens the city of the True Dharma. To the fleshly eyes of sentient beings, it appears as if unseen; yet for those who possess wisdom, it is clearly manifest.
He skillfully employed expedient means to once again open a quiet chamber on the sunny side of Mount Cuiyan. It was vast and spacious, a place of profound stillness and auspicious peace.

With all external conditions severed, his internal illumination was solely tranquil; he took the recitation and upholding of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* as his constant practice. He then lamented this precious stupa.
The Buddhas dwell together, manifesting the true aspect. If not me, who else? Leaning over paper and wielding the brush, I write with my hands and recite with my heart;

the formation of characters and the construction of forms are as exquisite as the operation of a loom. The tiers of the *cakra* (wheel-rim) rise in succession, the balustrades flow like water from a high roof, and their arrangement is both orderly and perfectly harmonious.
As if they had been born together, the Many-Treasures Stūpa and Śākyamuni face one another from time to time; from vast kalpas until now, they have not been separated by so much as a single thread.
While the sun and moon may come to an end, this stūpa shall endure forever. I vow to protect and maintain it, with devas and nāgas hastening forth, to bring about great benefit.
The supreme merit is peerless; I shall now offer words of praise. Like a painter joining seams, I extol the Great Being Mañjuśrī, who wears the grass robe and whose dark hair flows in loose tresses.
As he converses with Vimalakīrti on the Gate of Non-duality, there is not the slightest flaw in his mastery. Facing him...
Śākyamuni chose the Dharma of Perfect Penetration; how many roots must he have uprooted? Dropping the scripture from his hand, he utters "Svāhā" wherever he goes.
The morning sun facing the moon—two praises.
This person wears a tattered cotton robe, worn out and falling apart long ago. Today it cannot be mended; in what year will one ever take up the needle again?
Looking at which scripture? In a state of frantic haste, one merely opens and reads it. Failing to realize the primary meaning, one brings shame upon the moon at the edge of the sky.

Praise of Maitreya (The Eighteen Children): Having cast off the Tuṣita Heaven, he rolls into the ranks of children. He merely holds fast to his staff, unaware that he has lost his cloth bag. I bow my head to the World-Honored One Maitreya; when did he ever attain great sovereignty? Turning his head and twisting his brain— *Note:

This is a Zen verse (geju) attributed to the Ming dynasty master Xutang Zhiyu. It plays on the iconography of Maitreya as a chubby child carrying a staff and a cloth bag (pudai), which contains all the teachings of the Buddha.*
How pitiable! His own house has its own connoisseurs who love it.
This mute girl’s praise is but a single field; why sweep it so repeatedly? If she did not seal her mouth, how could she speak to others?
Master Puhua praises that which is ordinarily impenetrable to even the prick of a needle: "The iron walls and silver mountains are not yet solid.
At the twelve street corners he shakes his wooden clapper; he presents the whole platter before people.
The Patriarch Bodhidharma praised the vanguard of this eastern land;
yet behind the hall of the Western Heaven, his words offended the King of Liang, and his affairs were like being hampered by a hitched sleeve. Like a hollow reed drifting aimlessly upon the waves.
This does not mean to hide one's person while looking around at the vast emptiness; rather, one must fold one’s hands. The "one flower and five petals" blow the spring breeze from beyond kalpas;
the "direct pointing and single transmission" overturns the stone mortar in mid-air. Shen Guang cut off his own arm seeking peace of mind—a pity that he fought to expose the family’s disgrace.
The Chan Master Zhijue composed a eulogy for the Abbot of Fuhui Hermitage, Monk Renning, of Fenghua. He brought the portrait of Zhijue he had received to show it to me;
upon beholding it and paying my respects, I could not help but shed tears. I regret that I did not live at the same time as the Master, so that I might have sought to serve him.
I take up his brocade handkerchief and fly-whisk, listening as he grasps the great principles and expounds the profound tenets, exhausting my own subtle attachments to dharmas.
With utmost reverence, I bow my head to the ground and offer this praise:
The mind is without arising or ceasing; it is known only through direct realization. High up the mirror of the school is raised; when the light appears, the reflection follows.

At the top of a hundred-foot pole, one lets the body go with ease. Great function blazes forth, utterly transcending all dualities. Through the hundred-and-eight skillful means, one practices peacefully day after day.
Taking pity on those later students who diligently reap what they have idly plowed, he investigated his teachings as Yu studied the taming of the waters; how admirable is the cessation of the dew!
His words are devoid of empty praise.
Chan Master Hongzhou Huqiu Long praises [the tiger]:
"The meat-drunk intoxication has not yet sobered; its claws and fangs have already revealed their full edge. Killing people and bringing people to life is like empty space devouring empty space."
In Yuanwu’s chamber, he lost his strategic edge; atop Tiger Hill, he cursed the rain and scolded the wind. The luster of refined gold paled before him;
a single branch of peach blossoms vied for its crimson. Rolling the iron drum and casting the golden bell, he received the true lineage of Yangqi.
Master Ying’an’s Praise: "Alas!
This ancient master, throughout his life, delighted in causing a ruckus. He plowed the garden of thorns and sowed the seeds of the three poisons everywhere."
To claim you would continue the true lineage of Yangqi is much like opening one's eyes and yet dreaming.
Had I not obtained that single tattered robe at that time, I would have known you were destined to die of hunger and cold.
Master Yokawa’s eulogy for the Old Man:
Throughout his life, his speech was stammering; yet when he spoke, his words toppled Mount Sumeru. Few in India or here in this land knew him;
at the mountain hermitage of Mount Mō, he closed his gate in solitude.
Master Jizhao’s eulogy says: "Alas!
What an immeasurable great man! His words strike terror into one's very marrow. Throughout his life he sought only to leave people in a state of total blindness;

even Buddhas and Patriarchs could hardly approach him. It was said that his eye of wisdom lacked clarity, such that when viewing the bright moon-jewel or the lustrous night-gem, he failed to see them."
He was worth only half a coin; it was said that his skillful means were lacking in loftiness. Yet at times he would pick up Mount Sumeru and weigh it at twelve *liang*.
For twenty years he sat firmly under Lingxiao, and he galloped about like dragons and elephants throughout the four seas.

Therefore, he alone was able to cause the true lineage of Linji to rise majestically and to kindle the final flames of Wumiaoji. Through heaven and earth and across ten thousand ages, he remains equal to the void.
He is one whose lifespan is equal to that of empty space.
Zen Master Xuechuang praised the true monk Benchuan:
"His skull is distinct; he is of a single, harmonious temperament, yet thoroughly discerning. He has cast aside the thorny brambles."
The weeds are pulled out; the nails and stakes are removed. In the sixth month, clear frost descends; from the red furnace, white snow flies.
This causes Tianyushan to preserve its traces in two places. These traces, though empty, constitute Great Sameness. The wind follows the tiger, and the clouds follow the dragon.
Eulogy for Master Guding (Half-Body Portrait):

This fellow originally has no face or features; he has never been captured in a likeness, yet he is the primordial reality. He desires only that people of this age know he exists, and does not wish to reveal his full body.
This wondrously luminous mind-seal reflects the earth and illuminates heaven—who cares about those who lose their heads and mistake reflections for reality? It is pure black lacquer.
The Bamboo Rake. It overturns the seas and mountains; it truly exhausts the law until no people remain. It earns the hatred of men and the fear of men.
Only Miaoxi could serve as its progenitor, and Jizhao could be its immediate successor.
As for the rest of those masters who prattle of the profound and the subtle, peddling their own family style—how could they possibly race alongside or drive abreast with this?

Master Shanshi praises his seated meditation upon the simple couch. His mind is free from attachment, yet he responds mysteriously to myriad stimuli. He benefits others and improves the world; he has attained the orthodox lineage of Bodhidharma and continues the distant heritage of Kāśyapa.
He has obliterated the distinctions between past, present, and future, and widely propagated the precepts, concentration, and wisdom. Truly, he is the [Dharma] King of the Western Heaven.
O Son of the Buddha! He is the Awakened Sovereign of the Eastern Land.
The Reverend Master of the Southern Hall (invited by Xiyin of Longquan) praised him thus:
"His wisdom is like a gushing spring; his spiritual faculty is like a flash of lightning. He gazes with pride upon Deshan and Linji, and lets pass the Buddhas of the Sun-Face and Moon-Face."

Striking the sand-basin, the sound pierces the nine heavens; singing songs of liberation from delusion, the melodies must undergo a thousand transformations. Sitting firmly, he cuts off the orthodox command throughout all of Wu;
drawing the Dragon Spring from its scabbard, its radiance blazes forth.

Eulogy on the Image of a Flourishing and Withered Tree (Sitting Beneath a Withered Tree) The spring breeze fans the wild flowers into a blur; Seeking fragrance and plucking leaves, they fill the paths. When skin and flesh have fallen away, the reality remains;
I love this old tree and sit cross-legged here for a while.
Self-Praise (Requested by Elder Cuisanding):
One stroke of the top-knot [seal] encompasses both heaven and earth; fundamentally formless, how could brush and ink find a resting place? The three barriers are grandly opened.

Xiaohuanglong employs the compassionate heart of an old woman; a single shout, thundering like a storm. He finds Linji’s drumming for rice and gruel vulgar; when crossing a bridge, one must break the bridge.
Casting gold as a stake—how does it compare to casting tiles? The old tale of the eyebrows is joyfully reunited;
the green cliffs rise loftier by a thousand fathoms of emerald.
Furthermore, Yanwu requested that we not read the books of Eastern Lu, nor seek to understand the meaning of the Westward Transmission. With a single blow of the mallet, he shattered the sand pot;
let it fill the valleys and ditches as it may. Taking up the dried dung pellet with his hand, he made it permeate heaven and scorch the earth. Such was his way of teaching people.
There is something truly extraordinary here. Were it not for my friend Wuzhuo, who on this earth would recognize you? Alas!
Even if you were beaten to death, even a dog would not eat you; what more can be said of your so-called cultivation or your aspirations to realize the stage of *avaivartika*?

Furthermore, when the Venerable Jiaozhi originally invited [the Master] to the assembly on Mount Ling, the mind was transmitted with a single laugh; at the peak of Shaoshi, he attained the following by means of three prostrations.
These were all encounters on narrow paths where one runs into an enemy or a creditor—a dead snake being handled as if alive, "you are not my equal," or a fierce tiger captured alive.
"I am not your equal. Six rings of golden tin fly close to heaven, completely obscuring the pupils of the eyes of people of this age.
Inscription by the junior disciple Weiji Zong for Huihao and others. Compiled.

The Inscription on the Perfect Circle: Its essence and nature are empty and perfect. Who can fathom its beginning or end? Fundamentally it has no form or parts; how could it abide by rules and measures? Like the moon suspended in the sky, it is neither partial nor biased.
