A torrent! The sharpness of their rhetoric and the array of their pens are but mere clamor and noise. The sun and moon cast their reflections, interlacing and arraying one another;

above and below, they melt together, coalescing into waves of radiant color. Such is the natural brilliance of this literature: without moving a tongue, it turns forth the four great rivers. Vast and expansive, it is without end or limit;
the hundred streams all return to it, for its flavor is but one. Those who seek to fathom it with a ladle wish to ask for the ford, yet they gaze out at the ocean... toward [the vast expanse].
If the hairs on your body stand on end with cold,

I shall present you with the Great Canon and the Minor Canon of King Bimbisāra, their eight facets brilliant and clear, turning at a single push— how could there be any comparison between east and west before the Peak of Jade Rest?
Shaking the sounding-stick and striking the bell atop Mount Sumeru—every stroke benefits beings according to their capacity; at every turn, the blind and deaf are enlightened.
With a single toss, the great trichiliocosm is transformed thirty times over; the wind follows the tiger, and the clouds follow the dragon.
The Venerable Xian seeks admonition;
for a monk, the matter of traveling on pilgrimage is indeed no small cause. With diligent and tireless effort, let his every action and thought strive to equal that of Xian.
Since the water buffalo has not yet been tamed, how could one refrain from lashing it with a whip? Since worldly toil has not yet been cast off, how can it be called pure meditation?
For forty years at Yongquan, there were still many shifts and changes; only after forty years at Xianglin did he finally attain perfection.
If even the ancients were thus, how could it be otherwise for people today? It is like one who thirsts for water and digs a well on high ground:
as one digs deeper and deeper, one will surely encounter clear spring water. I am old and should remain behind; you, being young and strong, must press forward.
Repeatedly I exhort you; repeatedly I urge you on.
This short song is offered to Attendant Lian:
"The lotus flower blooms in the midst of the heavens. These words of the ancients were not spoken in vain. Throughout his life, Han Tui was vast and unobstructed.
The Jade Well merely boasts of its ten-fathom depth; within the hollows of lotus fibers, a great Peng bird soars.
On the tip of a slender lotus leaf, Mount Sumeru is as light as a palm; a handless immortal plucks the fruit and eats it. The fine-browed stone maiden’s flesh and bones are fragrant.
O Lotus-Meditator, Lotus-Meditator! Pray, break off a blossom for me. As you go along, do not say that those who understand you are few.
A Single Stanza on the Joy of Dwelling in the Mountains, Presented to the Librarian Jangjang:

How wonderful it is to dwell in the mountains! How wonderful it is to dwell in the mountains! The joy of dwelling in the mountains—who can speak of it? I see that the joy of dwelling in the mountains is manifold.
In old age, I regret not having resided in the mountains sooner. I recall the affairs of my early years of traveling on foot;
I ran east and west with no plan, visiting the gates of every master. Yet the ground of my mind remains as unclear as before. Sometimes they administered blows, sometimes they shouted;
sometimes they enticed or threatened me with sweet words. I did nothing but copy their patterns like drawing a gourd from a model, yet within the gourd there was nothing.

A true medicine; from this point on, it causes people’s illness to deepen further. Meeting with the "Mòxìng" (the Drowning Spirit), one encounters it once more. It is good to dwell in the mountains—it is truly good to dwell in the mountains!
Who can speak of the joy of dwelling in the mountains? The howling of monkeys and the singing of birds are the total presentation;

the valleys arrayed and peaks gathered are themselves the Triple Gem. The True Source and the Real Mark are revealed in full majesty; noble understanding and ordinary sentiment are swept away alike. Receive this in tranquility.

Cut off all contrived arrangements; for now, avoid seeking it from the mouths of others. Fellow practitioners, do not be hasty in your reports. Without clarifying the discourse on the mind-ground, you dwell in the mountains.
Yet, dwelling in the mountains only serves to increase your afflictions.
The One Smile Pavilion takes the fundamental principle as its core:
walking within the One Smile Pavilion, one returns again to sitting. The green mountains and white clouds cannot be spat upon; the six gates are void and still, utterly free from a speck of dust.

A copper water pitcher is placed according to the sūtras. When the World-Honored One held up the flower before the assembly at Vulture Peak, the hundreds of thousands of dragon-elephants were merely spectators.
How simple-minded! The golden-colored *dhūta* alone understands the matter. With a sudden laugh, he raises his eyebrows; to whom can he entrust the true meaning within that smile?
The stubborn Yangqi did not grant his approval. When a guest arrives, there is no need for further hesitation;
one should immediately recognize the master of the hall.
A Gift for Attendant Qiú of Dōnglín:

The celestial sphere and the jade of Biàn are auspicious omens for the world. When encountered by the noble, they are deemed base; when met by the lowly, they are deemed precious. The treasures of the mountain peaks are utterly unlike these.
Who dares to gaze directly upon them in their blazing brilliance? I laugh at the eighteen worthies of Mount Lú; amidst the sound of the lotus-water clock, they have opened [the gates].
The eyes sleep; only Yuanming alone understood how to perceive the opportune moment. With a fleeting frown, he simply departed. You, Master, have come from the mountains in person;
I, an old man, need not raise this topic again and again. An iron ox has plowed through the skin of my tongue; though you have a mouth, do not drink the waters of the West River.
The hermitage named Zhai (Sugar Cane Hermitage) does not plant pines around its buildings; it does not plant bamboo around its buildings. Around the buildings, only sugar cane seedlings are planted.

This is so that the distant descendants of Śākyamuni may continue their lineage through them. When a monk comes to knock at the door, there is nothing to say; clenching a coarse fist, he strikes the chest, demanding: "Do you understand?"
From now on, having seen the fundamental root, turn back and do not bite into the sweet fruit. One joint lower, one joint higher; from the beginning, there have been no idle branches.
Heaven-born, naturally sufficient in flavor; even weeding requires the application of diligent labor.
Last night the west wind rose in the forested clouds; with a whistling sound, the autumn wind battles the window paper. I urge the gardener to hasten his efforts!
Gathering up the true seeds of former years, he presents them to Tianxu, the West Hall Abbot.
"Daming raises the mountain-clearing axe; empty space claps its hands and Mount Sumeru dances. Daming then sets down the mountain-clearing axe.

The axe. Nanquan does not beat the drum of Yanguan; lifting it and letting it go, all is free. A fierce tiger escapes its cage, a hawk leaves its harness. He exposes the old, frozen scum of every quarter;
he is not like those who wander between Jiajiao and Huating. The ancestral wind of Shaoshi has already fallen into decline;
he vigorously shakes the great net to continue the work of the predecessors. Men of Wuyue vie to watch his true command being enacted; he shakes the crown of the head.
He shook the golden bells.
He seized the staff held in the hands of Master Liang and firmly gripped it. "Before you have trodden the upward path of my house, the entire Great Canon of the Teachings shall be overturned."

[The Master] turned [the bowl]. Within the pure realm, sand and soil are scattered; from emptiness back to emptiness, there are phrases and non-phrases, gain and loss in profusion, right and wrong intermingling.
If one possesses exceptional brilliance, one divides the rabbit beneath the talons of a blue hawk, naturally ensnaring the ancient and covering the present.
What more need be said of purity and defilement? An empty room knows no shame; from head to toe, it reveals all.
When you can let go, you must let go; when you cannot let go, carry it away on your shoulder.
Next, in the style of Master Quanshi of the Heavenly Realm, I offer this verse to Venerable Zhang, the Steward, who speaks of Chan and speaks of the Way:
"If you obscure your own light and do not thoroughly cleanse yourself, how can this matter ever be revealed?"
Do you not see? Before Yunfeng entered the room of Dayu, the young son abandoned his father and fled. When the wooden band of the bucket burst, all his clever stratagems were exhausted;
from that moment, the "head-word" (huatou) was passed down and widely celebrated. And do you not see? Ying’an once served as the Hall Superintendent;
his legacy remains uniform to this day, like a single stroke of a brush. Within the cave, the peach blossoms retain their springtime; for sixty minor kalpas, the wind [has never ceased].

The rain falls swiftly. Hereafter, when you are born, be careful never to follow others away. From the highest barrier-gate, I have completely blocked the way. The dragon-river bowl-bag weighs a thousand *qun*;
I, the Old Man, shall meet you and personally entrust it to you.

In the provisional middle, lightness and heaviness may be adjusted; what is there to adjust within the middle? Within the provisional middle, the Way must surely exist. For nine years he faced the wall, yet fell into calculation;
reclining beneath the vine-shade, his efforts were in vain. To recognize the perfect and constant, which does not lean to one side: it is like the vast, deep autumn sky, where nothing remains.
Fine dregs. Just at midnight, the lunar disc stands alone; it cannot yet be lightly compared to this.

Although Hanshan’s eyes and brain are sharp and clear, when he picks up the scale, there is originally no star upon its tail. Half a catty is exactly eight ounces—it never deviates. Clapping his hands and laughing aloud, he returns to his mountain retreat.
Before the Great Image at Xinchang, the facial features of Bodhisattva Asanga had become damaged.
The Venerable Ying raised funds through his spiritual influence to restore its adornments.

He spoke a verse to show that Maitreya appears from time to time, and that Asanga is in constant companionship with him; thus, following this teaching, his head and face were transformed from beginning to end.
Without departing from his original body, the nostrils remain as they were, pointing downward; who would say there are no tendons within the eyes?

The stone city’s green mountains are carved like jade; Mirror Lake’s white waters float like silver. This is precisely the Inner Court of Tuṣita, solemn and majestic, without the slightest speck of dust intervening.
Why wait for the dragon’s head to blossom before preaching the Dharma to save sentient beings? *Du!* (A shout).

Sending off the Abbot of the Zhejiang Tripitaka to return to his hometown—failing to understand Chan meditation or the Way, he focuses his mind solely on how good it would be to go home. How much delusion and ignorance of one's own fundamental nature!
Truly so. Relying on one's own home and neighboring dwellings, one grows old in vain. You have recognized the essential pivot in recent years;

you know how to eat, dress, and discern what is right and wrong. Why then do you still travel the old paths? Grasping the whole within the palm, you have made a hasty departure. The ancients had models for returning to their hometowns;
it is not that people today lack the capacity to let go and take up. When Yongjia raised his staff and arrived at Caoxi, he stayed for but a single night.
This return was no mere recklessness. Furthermore, when Yuanwu returned to the City of Brocade, the elders and commoners together prepared a tea banquet to welcome him.

His Way shone with light and his virtue glowed for a thousand ages; bright as the white sun suspended in the azure heavens. To return home in such a manner is truly not bad; to do otherwise would be a mistake.
This is why Dongshan chose not to return after death—he wished to cause later generations to follow the example of the former sages.
A man of spirit breathes forth a ten-thousand-fathom rainbow; why consent to grease the axle of a swift steed to follow old tracks?

Smash through the dark ghost-cave of the past; you must support the True Teaching with bare hands. With spring winds and spring rains on the Tiantai path, the river flows in a hundred folds like a spread-out cloth.
To plant your feet firmly upon the ground is the true advantage; do not envy others crossing the river by floating their straw hats.

The Source of Mind was composed for the Head Seat Jiu; the Source of Mind has neither shallow nor deep. To attempt to investigate it is merely to suffer in vain. It is simply a matter of overturning it so that not a drop remains;
only then may one be permitted to come and inquire about its ford. Please do not clamor, my friend, but listen as I sing of the Source of Mind: it surges beyond the heavens.

Flooded like the sun, it spans from antiquity to the present; it raises the pure and stirs up the turbid, forgetting center and periphery. The Tathāgatas of the three periods do not know its existence;

they have been soaked by it until their nostrils are pierced through. Facing each other clearly, they do not recognize one another; a sword hangs between their brows, its light shimmering brilliantly.
One may seek peace through its source, yet find no peace; from the three-inch tongue, thunderclaps resound.
Master Yuan Zang cultivates the illusory chamber;
after awakening, he seeks his dream-scape before his eyes. He gallops swiftly toward the sun, hoping to leave behind a shadow. If a shadow could be left behind, then a dream might be preserved.

Investigate! Even an illusion can be cultivated, but one must examine oneself. Using an illusory mind to cultivate illusory dharmas—the roots of illusion are deep and firm, and in the end, they are difficult to uproot.
Once the doors and gates are all opened wide, my house finally realizes that heaven and earth are vast. Sitting upright on a simple couch, as stable as a mountain;
when inspiration strikes, I casually play the stringless lute. Among its melodies, there is one tune most ancient. One should go seek out a knower.
The sound continues the legacy of the ancestors.

To the abbot Yizang of Baizhang, it reveals the ultimate barrier beyond the ordinary: pierced through in every direction from ancient times to the present, there is not even the space of a hair between them. If one can realize it before a word is spoken, one has attained it.
It is like treading upon two diverging paths; though one may later master the phrasing, one only grasps a single fragment.

Old Bāng, that ancient adept, needlessly creates complications by pointing out a wild fox—its stench fills the vast void. "Not falling into cause and effect": ice flakes scattered across the long streets under a scorching sun. "Not obscuring cause and effect":
the fragrance of lotus flowers wafting through the month of December amidst the flames. A man of the Way is truly eminent.
The stream flows; the place of attainment is spontaneously transcended. The Great Hero Peak is toppled, and the ten directions resound with clamor.
When you realize the time of passing the imperial examination with an empty mind, the cinnabar cassia of the moon palace will be uprooted along with its roots.
Wanzong styled himself "One Who Severs the Buddha-Seed. He requested a verse:
"The methods of one who severs the Buddha-seed are distinct: from within a furnace of blazing flames, he plucks out snow. Even the Ten Sages and Three Worthies do not approach it;
how could the Śrāvakas of the Lesser Fruit even be ranked among it? His daily conduct and concealment are truly marvelous; he has transcended the vast primordial void."
Xīyí (Silent and Unperceivable). Not receiving the formal prediction from Dīpaṃkara, he naturally did not err by even a hair’s breadth.

Those who cling to the Dharma and wander in delusion do not realize their mistake; a mangy dog laughs at the crane in the clouds. Turning the Wheel of Dharma amidst piles of paper money, attaining Perfect Enlightenment at a table of pork.
Wearing the Vajra-jewel sword high upon his girdle, it strikes terror into others with its chilling radiance. The Buddha has none—
"What need is there to sever the spiritual lineage? To have a lineage that can be severed would result in the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.
Thus spoke Fayu to Venerable Xian.
Lücheng Xian, the *karmadāna*, visited me at Taibai Mountain Hermitage to inquire about the maladies of Chan. I said, "Chan is fundamentally without malady;
it is because those who practice Chan fail to grasp its subtle essence that Chan itself becomes a malady."
If one possesses great roots and is of great capacity, directly taking up the seeds and grasses of unsurpassed Bodhi, they will naturally differ from the ordinary.

Amidst the daily activities of concealment and manifestation, they remain solemn and majestic; they ensure that the five desires and eight winds, the four modes of birth and nine realms of existence, as well as Bodhi, Nirvana, True Suchness, liberation, and all dharmas, cannot come near them. It is thus with all such dharmas.

This is precisely the sickness of sick Chan. If one can decisively cut it off at the head, being inwardly like wood or stone and outwardly like empty space—vast, clear, and pure—then even Chan cannot be found, let alone sickness. In recent times, the school’s style has not flourished;
the essentials of direct pointing have often degenerated into frivolous discourse. Those who occupy the "curved bench" and claim the title of patriarch merely seek to ensnare the new generation.
Study [this]: take all those words that the ancients used to point directly to people—words that penetrate to the very bone and marrow—and bring them forth.
It is like an old village teacher instructing young students to recite the "Shang Daren" (The Great Man Above);
one phrase is a word for seizing the opportune moment, one phrase is a word of approval or disapproval, and one phrase is a word of resonance.
As for "words," a single phrase that does not fall into the realm of the profound and mysterious is a secret deliberation taken as the fundamental principle;
one transmits it to another, which is called "transmitting the Dharma to save sentient beings. Such base and inferior matters need not be enumerated.
If you are truly one who is determined to shoulder this burden, you need not seek others to speak of the "disease of Zen"; simply take a step back and look beneath your own heels.
Investigate this intimately and profoundly; will there not come a time when you reach the destination?
To Venerable Ying, [the Master] showed that the Great Master of the Dharma had, from Prajñātāra, secretly obtained a seal without words, which he took to be the ultimate.
This supreme, peerless, and most precious treasure, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, was once briefly employed within the borders of the six heterodox schools in that land.

Deeming them unworthy vessels for its reception, I have now worn it upon my person and traveled eastward. Arriving at the Land of the Red District (Zhōngguó), I seek a person to whom I may transmit it.
Initially, I encountered the Son of Heaven of the Liáng house; however, those he esteemed were merely [the patterns of] insects and birds.

Zhuan. The tiger-shaped seal and the dragon [emblem]—the *li* sash were thus not joined. He eventually went to Shaolin, where he sat in cold seclusion for nine years, waiting for someone to come seek his instruction, having no intention of seeking out those who would receive it from him.
By chance, there was a certain monk who cut off his own arm and sought instruction amidst deep snow;
perceiving his earnestness, he took pity on him and granted him the transmission. From that point on, they passed it down to one another, such that none were unable to attain it.

Regarding the provisional establishment of the Dharma, there are few who are able to transcend the fundamental tenets and leap beyond conventional categories, wielding the teachings with such unconventional and horizontal mastery.

Yet when it came to Fengxue, his hands were shattered into a hundred fragments by a single blow from the other. To this very day, neither the sons nor the grandsons have been able to piece it back together.
Vinaya-master Ying of Jianchang, his heart filled with indignation and his mouth struggling for words, desires to reclaim the entirety of what was lost from Fengxue.
This "bottom seal" was brought forth by the Great Master Bodhidharma to let out a single breath;
it may truly be called a daring resolve that startles heaven and a brilliant strategy that surpasses the world. Yet you come to ask this old monk:
"What characters were carved within this seal at the beginning? I rebuked him, saying: "I have told you clearly—it is the 'seal of no-character. Are you still..."
Someone came to ask what characters were carved upon it.
It was shown to the Chan practitioner Zhide:
"The Great Master of Yongjia, after staying one night at Caoxi, later composed the *Song of Realizing the Way*. As soon as he opened his mouth, he said: 'Cease...'"
Study to become a person of the Way who practices non-action and idleness; do not eliminate deluded thoughts, nor seek after truth.

Furthermore, there is no profound or mysterious Buddha-dharma to be discussed. As for the many things explained extensively in what follows—this constant clamor and distress is nothing but commentary;

it is simply the four characters "absolute study and non-action. If one were to personally awaken to and personally realize this in a single morning, one would be uniquely liberated and independent. Not...

If one can transcend the idle realms and conditions of past sages and no longer cling to the ordinary, everyday functions of one’s own household, then walking hand-in-hand with Yongjia will not be difficult.
When Yaoshan visited Shitou, one day while they were sitting together, Shitou asked, "What are you doing?
Yaoshan replied, "I am doing nothing at all. Shitou said, "In that case, you are just idly sitting. Yaoshan replied, "Indeed I am."
If you sit in leisure, that itself is it. Look at those who have attained it:
even this very sitting in leisure cannot bind them, let alone the Vinaya precepts, discourses on the scriptures, or the oral transmissions of the masters.
Since this is so, how could they ever be willing to seek falsely outwardly? Do not say there is nothing to be found outwardly.

Seeking is simply looking inward; when has there ever been anything there? Therefore it is said: "If a person cultivates the Way but the Way does not proceed, myriad perverse states will vie with one another to arise.
When the sword of wisdom is drawn forth, not a single thing exists; before the bright side is revealed, the dark side is already clear."
Although one person may eat a meal, how can this cause all people to be satiated?
If you should hesitate even for a moment or pause your mental activity, Master Yongjia has long since passed beneath your very heels.
To the Attendant Dandan:
When the Great Master Bodhidharma first arrived in the Eastern Land, he spoke only of "directly pointing to the human mind, seeing one's nature, and attaining Buddhahood.
At that time, as soon as he uttered these words, he felt his own tongue had already become as heavy as a thousand *jin*. How could it be compared to the lack of fundamental basis found today?
The fundamental reason is that they run outwardly after things, drawing parallels and making comparisons, pointing east and painting west. They ask, "Which public case is for the sake of others?
Which public case is not for the sake of others? Thus they corrupt students, saying, "I am a descendant of Bodhidharma."
To transmit and uphold the direct pointing to the authentic source—alas! How could one possibly escape the karmic retribution for slandering the Dharma?
If this is a true patriarch, he is like a lion crouching on the ground, like a fierce tiger emerging from the forest; there is no place for you to stroke him, and no place for you to draw near.
Even if it were the Great Master Bodhidharma himself who arrived here, you must still press him once. Although we have reached this point...
One must not treat this lightly. It is unmistakably something forged from solid steel and cast from raw iron;

only then does it possess a direction, only then does it possess the capacity for speech. Among all those who have studied the Way throughout past and present, none has surpassed Linji in transcending his peers.
When he was in Huangbo’s assembly, he asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma three times and was beaten three times, receiving sixty blows each time.
Even the staff was set aside in avoidance; had it not been for the high-placed, talkative old master who provoked him, how many opportunities would have been lost?
Then, awakening from the dream and realizing his error, he struck himself in the ribs with his fist—though it may be said that he stroked the tiger’s whiskers backward.
They have already passed by as thieves with their bows drawn; how much more so for those who point to a deer as a horse, or recognize a servant as their lord?

Attendant Xin understands this matter thoroughly, so there is no need for further repetition. You shall not be permitted to handle the great affairs; each person must attend to their own minor matters.
To the Keeper of the Collection:
Generally speaking, in the study of the Way, once one has a place of rest, there is a path to be pursued.
If there were no place of rest, where could such pursuit be applied? For instance, space is fundamentally without name or form, yet people insist on establishing them for it.
Regarding names and forms: as soon as they exist, there is already a vision of voidness, stillness, vastness, and profound breadth.

When practitioners of the Way apply their full strength toward the matter of their own fundamental nature, it is like beating a drum while searching for a lost son; they only become increasingly estranged from it.
This is why Deshan would strike a monk the moment he entered the gate, and Linji would likewise act upon a monk’s entry.
"Ha! It is just like a state weapon: it is used only when there is no other choice. Later, however, people followed the stream while losing the source, needlessly creating complications;

they instead provided commentaries on the "stick" and the "shout," saying, "If you understand, then you will know that Deshan’s stick does not issue from the hand, and Linji’s shout does not issue from the mouth," thereby directing students to search for meaning within these very words.
Even if you were to investigate and find [the truth], how would it differ from driving ants to a postal station or employing mosquitoes to carry a mountain?
Have you not seen what the Chan Master Changsha said: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, because they have been identifying with the conscious mind since time immemorial.
This is the root of birth and death throughout countless kalpas; the deluded call this the 'Original Person'."

This refers precisely to this. From his youth, the Abbot of Lingyin, Wuzhu, entered the monastic forests and attended upon spiritual mentors (*kalyāṇamitra*), thoroughly investigating and clarifying his own fundamental matter.
He was most proficient in the study of the *Yijing* (Book of Changes). Consequently, [the Master] cited a verse by Changsha and followed it with a question, saying:
"As for what is said in the *Yijing*, 'Tranquil and unmoving, yet responding and thereby penetrating,' is this the root of birth and death, or is it not?"
Wuzhu said, "A tiger bites a great beast; a snake swallows a turtle's snout. I said, "This is precisely the root of birth and death.
Wuzhu merely shook his hand back and forth. I have recorded this here as well, for thirty years hence, empty talk will prevail.
It is not necessarily the case that this does not arise from such causes.

To the great Chan practitioner and those who study the Way today: if you do not clarify the Great Way but instead devote yourselves solely to greedy seeking, it is just like striking at the very moment one first resolves to begin their practice.
To understand the Way through conceptual interpretation is already to err. Now, as for the Way, it is the Way of primordial purity.
From vast kalpas past until this very day, it has neither gain nor loss, neither newness nor antiquity, neither light nor darkness, and neither form nor name.
It does not increase among the Buddhas, nor does it decrease among sentient beings; yet we forcibly name it "the Way"—this is already a defilement.
If one says that there is something to be accomplished through the method of learning, this is what is called an error.

In antiquity, those who could not help but do so called those who transcend the ordinary "men of the Way" (xué dào rén). This was because they took "having nothing to learn" as their learning, and "having nothing to speak of" as their Way.
Having nothing to learn means there is no attachment; having nothing to speak of means there is no compliance. In the midst of casual speech, they might inadvertently utter the word "Buddha."
Master Zizhu said: "One must rinse one's mouth for three years before one can truly be called a practitioner of the Way.
The Venerable Nanquan said: "The Way does not belong to knowledge, nor does it belong to non-knowledge. Knowledge is deluded perception; non-knowledge is indeterminate ignorance.
If one truly penetrates the Way that is free from doubt, it is like the vast void—how could one forcibly impose right and wrong? "Is this not the teaching of Master Wang?"
They sacrifice their bodies for the sake of sentient beings, disregarding their own peril and death; yet they do not realize that within the treasury of our King, there is no such blade.
Ancient sources speak of the vast and boundless waves prior to the Kalpa of Awesome Sound (Vibhāṣa), but after Śākyamuni, not a single drop remains. Even if you were to head toward those waves—
Where the waves are vast and the waters boundless, one must firmly grasp the secure barrier so that no leakage occurs; yet this is precisely to lose the source and forfeit the root.
Furthermore, if one attempts to open a single vein where not even a drop exists, the waters will drench the sun and flood the heavens, resulting only in fallen dew adding to the current.
To depart from these two paths and engage in some other practice means that you have not yet attained the capacity to leap across our Caoxi Road.
Have you not seen it? When Zhaozhou visited Zhunyu, he carried his staff up into the Dharma Hall; looking east and looking west, Zhunyu asked, "What are you doing?
Zhaozhou replied, "Probing the water. Zhunyu said, "In here, there is not even a single drop to probe. Probing...

"What is this? Zhaozhou leaned his staff against the wall and departed. Zhaozhou’s *zhuyou* (jujube) tree takes up that moment when yin and yang had not yet been distinguished and heaven and earth had not yet taken form;
it scoops up these surging, overflowing, and primordial waters and pours them from one to another.
This may be called knowing the source and the course, and attaining their depth and shallowness—compared to which, measuring with a ladle or probing with a gnat is but a distant prospect.
How vastly different is Yangxiang Ruofu’s kind from this—like the distance between clouds and mud!

Nevertheless, while it may be possible to exhaustively fathom that which is vast and surging like waves prior to the Era of Awesome Sound (Weiyin), it is not permitted to exhaustively fathom that which is utterly devoid of even a drop after the time of Śākyamuni.
Why is this so? Have you not heard it said: "The waves of Caoxi are just like [those of the ocean]?"
Countless commoners have been submerged by the land. The monk Xing of Linchuan, styled Guyuan, requested an explanation from me;
before I knew it, my heart was filled with distress.
*The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shu Zhong*, Volume Five.
The Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shuzhong, Volume Six,
Compiled by the Monk-Qiūngsuì and Others. Five-Syllable Verse (Wuyan Lü).

Master Jizong resided at Xitang, harboring a long-standing vow to uphold the Dharma. For forty years he labored with diligence; his verses were so pure they could serve as offerings to the Buddhas, and his deeds were so white they could be inscribed upon heaven.

Seated in meditation, his hempen robes were thin; walking in contemplation, the snow atop his head was rounded. As the light of the morning star was about to fade, a single lamp was transmitted within the inner courtyard.
On a day of leisure, I read the five verses sent by Master Zhenjing to High Sheriff Gao of Jingnan.
I admire how he directly reveals the Dharma of the mind, like clouds spreading across the sky, leaving not even a hair’s breadth of concealment.
This is truly the skillful means of one who wields the great drum and banner. I have thus composed verses in his rhyme to show them to Attendant Fu.
The fundamental mind has no self-nature; cease debating host and guest. Delusive thoughts are dogs on the trail; cleverness is the hunter.
Following one another in shared accord, their calls and responses are most intimate. Once the prize is won and returned home, all may roam freely in the state of true suchness.

Cognition and vision return to cognition and vision; why must one recognize them as the mind? The four modes of birth equally partake of their use; searching through the seven locations is but a vain pursuit.

The wise and enlightened remain ultimately steadfast and prominent, while the ignorant and deluded drift further into obscurity. Suddenly recalling the matter of the Westward Journey, it moves me to profound lamentation.
Vigilant activity follows a different path; silent illumination falls into deviant Chan. Ants swarm at the scent of meat; monkeys and baboons cling to trees.
A corpse lies sleeping in the tomb at night; rotten seeds are sown in the autumn fields. Such are the essentials of the enlightened mind—know that you may not yet have realized them.

This very face given by one's mother: do not seek it elsewhere in the midst of time. It stands forth alone as the eye of the thousand sages; it shines brilliantly as the heart of the ten thousand spirits.
Perfected purity is not caused by antiquity; leisurely wandering has never begun only now. Eons have passed in vain vastness; I can only lament their drifting and sinking.
Yangshan personally planted millet; Baizhang encouraged the opening of fields. Though they produced a thousand different forms, all return to the single flavor of Chan.
Though the mouth may verbally reproach and complain, the countenance remains perfectly composed. When there is no bright moon beneath the water, one should know that the moon is in the sky.
Ten recitations demonstrate the Dharma;

they purify the mind, awaken the source of concentration, and give rise to the aspiration for the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. By adding oil to assist the Buddha-lamp, the ten recitations are perfected in an instant, transcending the distant reaches of the three vehicles.
Celestial music plays from time to time; one ascends lotus pedestals at every step. Although Master Huiyuan has passed away, this Way must be propagated by worthy men.
A Verse on Seated Meditation for the Attendant Shishi:
Sitting is not true sitting; contemplating the mind is but deluded mind. When all streams are cut off together, the three periods of time naturally subside.
That flame has neither beginning nor end; its source is beyond depth or shallowness. Gold requires a hundred refinements; cherish and value the good moments of time.
Reading the poems of the eminent monks, I am shown the Heart-Seal (Cittamudrā).

The Way accords with the destiny of a thousand years; his person wanders through the forest of myriad practices. Profound words transcend mundane speech; deep contemplation gives rise to pure chanting.
The luster of jade is hard to match his virtue; the hardness of gold is but a vain comparison for his mind. Though there is no overt satire here, his righteous spirit remains dense and majestic.
Hearing crickets as dawn approaches, he sits amidst the masts; the cricket’s cry emerges from the forest. Clearly proclaiming the Patriarch’s intent, where in this could there be any ordinary mind?
Vividly, it dissolves my pure dreams; Leisurely, it aids my solitary chanting. All people of this age listen together; Who would say there are few who understand?

The heat blazes across the great earth, melting metal and stone, Yet the Zen mind remains only serene and calm. In profound stillness, there is no turbid thought; Amidst the dense world, one is naturally pure and empty.
Sitting upon rocks, he frequently brandishes his whisk; gazing at the stream, he watches the leaping fish. Leisurely wandering within the three realms, cold and heat concern him not.

I present this to one who has long dwelt in a mountain hut half-shrouded by clouds; he is diligent only in accumulating the wealth of the Dharma. He first filters the water before brewing tea, and as he eats congee, he immediately roasts moss.
Moss on the rocks forms clusters as it exudes; mountain flowers bloom petal by petal. Having no other concerns in my old age, I wait for the Golden Terrace in a single thought.
In mourning for my late elder brother, Master Dīyuán:
Though you passed away early, the resonance of your lineage still lingers. Your subtle conduct was strictly maintained in secrecy, and your realization of the ancestral gate was profound.

Refining gold from its ore; questioning with the precision of a needle piercing a mustard seed. As the year draws to a close, those who travel with me are few; upon whom can I rely to speak of this heart?

The world is as treacherous as wind and waves, yet in my lofty study I remain alone and serene. To sustain myself, I possess no superfluous things; to aid the teaching, I have but these remaining volumes.

Sitting long, the couch of mugwort has become riddled with holes; writing much, the iron inkstone has worn through. Knowing only how to propagate the ancestral Way, who would have thought it would cost me my natural years?

I recall in the past when we requested instruction together, while the former master was still in the vigor of his prime: before a single word had left his mouth, the hidden meaning was already known.
Seeking nothing further from others, he is ultimately able to sustain himself with dignity. Like a shady tree under heaven, it is the thickest branches that break first.

*Inscribed at the Mountain Dwelling of Master Gui:* Crimson leaves fill the pine paths; A clear stream winds through the bamboo grove. The west wind has aged my twin locks; The setting sun casts half the window in shadow.
Tattered robes are best suited to the cold; dwelling in seclusion, one never tires of depth. The verses left behind by the Indian Sage remain; unroll the scroll and chant them aloud.
Reading the words of Dongshan is like biting into an iron-acid dumpling—how much elegance there is in this! Watching puppets in the city, singing folk songs within the house.
The staff falls as rain from the blue sky; the lotus blooms in the twelfth month. The descendants follow the old ruts; who can see the shuttle that transforms into a dragon?
To the attendant Shicuo:
A single piece of flawless jade has long been mixed with common stones. When polished by a skilled hand, the distinction between the fine and the coarse is clearly discerned.
Secretly resembling military orders, he was refined in deliberating state strategies; had there been the slightest deviation from the standard, heaven and earth would have diverged.
Xie Jingzhong came to visit me while I was passing through;
I had cleared my traces amidst a thousand crags, and the wattle gate had long remained unopened. Just as the fresh rain had finished falling, I suddenly beheld an old friend arrive.

Roasted bamboo shoots are offered to the tea bowls; boiled mugwort is presented to the rice-cup. I wish to remain here with you to dwell together; let us divide the rocks to sit upon in their many layers.
The autumn sea cries out as the jade dew washes the void azure; the vast ocean is limpid and unshaken. Not even a single bubble has yet arisen—where can one find the full tide?

Suddenly the western wind blows fiercely; white waves cling to the heavens and rise high. Amidst the laughter and conversation of the old fisherman, he seizes a golden tortoise with a mere flick of his hand.

Presented to the West Hall Abbot Qian of Nanhu, who observes the essential meaning of the Taiheng school: The peaks of Song and Shao transmit only the mind; the Yangtze and Han rivers all return to the sea. The alms bowl and water flask are but a single gold.

Unable yet to realize through personal witness, how can one avoid competing in speculative inquiry? Three beasts cross the same river; according to their capacity, they reach depths both shallow and deep.
Inscribed at the Thatched Cottage of Mount Wang, built upon the Fu Creek:
The pine gate stands open day and night; though the household is poor, no thieves enter. The mountain is so beautiful that monks come to visit.
The leaking roof is re-thatched with straw; as the years pass, moss gradually accumulates. The pear and chestnut trees encircling the eaves were planted solely for the sake of one's descendants.
I send this to Mr. Yang Jianwen: we have not seen one another for five years.
Moreover, the roads are difficult to traverse. I hope you are at ease and know yourself to be free from much illness; I imagine your white hair is without streaks of gray.
The Mysterious Classic is complete upon the desk; the maiden returns within the incense burner. Without strings, there is true delight—just as when responding to Master Ma’s lute-playing.
To show this to those of superior capacity:
this Way is possessed by every person, yet those who truly realize it are rare. When explained, all have awakening; when pressed to the limit, none harbor doubt.
To recognize the intent of the single transmission, one must clarify the kōan of the "upward direction. Walking alone without a companion—this is truly the child of those who have left the home-life.
I present this Dharma of the Mind-Ground to Master Ke of Chufu-an: it was not transmitted at Shaolin; its secret meaning is manifest in every instance, and the true lamp burns everywhere.
One must know that the fires of the three poisons are precisely the supreme vehicle of Chan. If you do not yet understand the essential point, exert yourself within this moment.

A Parting Gift to Master Cheng on the Message from the West: I am not reluctant to discuss this with you. Who does not possess this in their very being? Each person is uniquely sovereign according to their own direction.
The later heaven becomes the grandfather; the ancient Buddha is the descendant. When young, strive diligently in study and pilgrimage; the passing years flee like a flash of lightning.

To the teacher’s disciple Tanwei: Above this, there is no mysterious path. When it is time to rest, one should simply rest. The lamp of wisdom shines eternally in stillness; the water of insight flows forever on.
The great earth shall ultimately come to an end; empty space knows neither departure nor staying. Within this time, one should exert effort; let not the years and months pass in vain.
In the same rhyme, I respond to the esteemed scholar Wu Caizhai:
Renowned is Master Wu, who dwells in the marketplace beside a willow grove. A *jiao* lute hangs high upon the wall; spring grasses fill the shade of the walls.

The reputation of the Way is as weighty as Mount Qiu; the source of your eloquence is as deep as the rivers and seas. What good fortune it is for this mountain monk to be granted the opportunity to discuss the mind with you.
A Heptasyllabic Regulated Verse Sent Off En Attendant Returning to Shu.
A master of the Chan school for a hundred generations in Western Shu; dragon-flying and phoenix-leaping, he appeared in his own time.

His cart was filled with the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* commentary, yet he also composed elegant little poems of unconventional grace. Before Mount Dòuzi, he beat a tile drum; outside the Grass-Sandals Hermitage, he covered a tortoise.
On this journey, do not fall into the tracks of others; establish new rules and sing the ancestral mechanism.
In the same rhyme, I respond to my Dharma brother Nantang’s verse sent to me:
The Chan exposition overwhelms the old Master Guifeng; From beneath his tongue, he perpetually blows the wind of Shaoshi. Beyond the realm of the thousand sages, he opens the True Eye;
Upon the tip of a single hair, he manifests spiritual powers. To smelt gold, he needs no yin-yang charcoal; To ensnare the phoenix, why require the net of heaven?
The Earth-Cage: Cutting off the idle proclamations of past and present, who in the Western Heaven or this land shares in this?
Again, using the same rhyme, I send this to Master Xibai:
Towering and precipitous, it rises above all other peaks; Who else can truly succeed to this solitary wind? His illustrious fame resounds like rolling thunder.
Zhen: His lofty eloquence flows like the vast expanse of the Milky Way. He must laugh at Jingqing picking up the fire-tongs; how could he tolerate Ganzi bowing before the steamer?
The Seal of the Wondrously Enlightened Mind has been transmitted for a long time; it is not the same as ordinary engraved seals.
On the fifteenth day of the first month, the *taeggu* drum was struck at Insan Hermitage. Master Muryong Mongtang offered a verse urging me to remain;
I respond in the same rhyme to express my gratitude.
Three strikes of the *taeggu* resound before the hall; I am ashamed of my lack of talent, yet I am honored by your refusal to let me go. The Way is lost and times are perilous; my heart grows weary.
Fragile is the body; the journey is long—rely on strength, for what more can be added? The green pine stands tall and upright with its thousand-year integrity;
the red hibiscus blooms in splendor for but a single day. Cherish the spiritual friend of Dragon Peak; a single word of his is sufficient to quell all clamor.
Next, following the rhyme of "Jièshì" (The Mustard Seed Room), two verses in lamentation for Master Nántáng:
Who knows to whose household he has become a horse or a donkey? Nántáng has ultimately made this his destiny. Do not say that the day of departure is not the day of arrival;

you must believe that the moment of birth is the very moment of death. As for me, your disciple, I shall only ensure the transmission of the bowl and robe; what need is there for the Brahma King to offer his tribute?
Flower branches: black pearls scattered out, three thousand in number; these too are once more settled upon the eyes and brows.
Xianchun’s proclamations were far too fragmented; father and son ring forth in resonance, vowing to meet the ancients.

Rekindling the lamp of the lineage to illuminate the world, he once again takes up the public case, his words startling the age. Utterly devoid of breath, they stir the nostrils; how could there be heart or liver hanging there?
A tree branch; a back-flip somersault beyond the three realms. The young lad Bingding smiles with upturned brows.
To see off Chan Master Chu as he departs to travel for study:
"In our school, there is no dharma to be transmitted or upheld. Wondrous function and spiritual powers—what need is there for a teacher? How swift it is, like riding a fine steed upon the highway!"
A horse—risky as a precipitous ravine, it restrains the azure dragon. Behold where the great ocean’s waves surge; this is precisely the moment when empty space shatters to pieces.
Once you have finished traveling extensively to consult the masters of wisdom, do not hesitate to come and receive the blow upon the crown of your head.
The attendant Fūsangdēng requested further instruction with a verse, which contained the line: "From thirty thousand *li* away, he comes to inquire about the Way.
I answered in the same rhyme:
"From thirty thousand *li* away, he comes to inquire about the Way; Having endured hardships to their full extent, who can truly know? Piteous indeed, he has lost the very midst of it."
The matter is simply this: because you crave too much and rush outward, honeyed water and sweet sugar are not good friends; the angry fist and the hot shout are your true teachers.
When you turn your body and step upon the path from whence you came, your eyes will already be firmly settled above your eyebrows.

A Record of the Completion of the Bathhouse for National Teacher Quanshi of Tientai, Verified by the Opening of the Hall by Master Zongyi: It is intended to cause the minds of weary beings to become clear.

Having recognized that the heat of summer is like fire, one further knows that the heat within is as cold as ice. Where there is no merit, merit can be established; where it is difficult to record, it is recorded. Where there is defilement, that defilement may be removed.
Rebirth. No matter how you, Gu-ling, may rub your back with your hand, once you have arrived, how could you dare to present such a haphazard display?
[This is] a verse in the same rhyme, sent to my Dharma-nephew Mie-zong and the two West Hall Attendants Shi-tian:
Our aging faces have each become those of old men; The eyes are already clouded and the ears are deaf. Suddenly receiving your letter, I am honored by its profound kindness.

I think: When shall we join hands and speak of our former lineage? The wind and moon of the mountain forests remain as they were of old; the talent of those by the rivers and seas is naturally different.
Those who were my companions in days past are few today; only now do I realize the true appearance of the mountains after autumn.
Lamenting the Former Master Puci of Dailin:

The Merit of the Successive Patriarchs Equals Their Own Since Youth; in Old Age, There Is No Further Need for the Whip. Though the Three Turnings of the Dharma-Wheel are called wondrous, the Single Transmission of the Essential School does not fall into the abstruse.
The wind is high in the maritime land—no dreams reach it; at the end of the year, there is [the peak] atop the Cloud-Peak.

The records and commentaries have, in their final stages, leaked the essential meaning of returning to the source. After the fire, the stalks of *máohuì* grass stand green, brushing against the heavens.
Next, the principles extend across the primordial limit;
the lineage of Shaoshi is not easily discussed. Only when life is fully preserved and death is fully enacted does one startle the multitude. Try looking at Linji’s study under Huangbo.
Huangbo still envies Yangqi’s reception of Baiyun; though he was struck on the palm and the cheek, he ultimately accepted it himself. Who else has heard of the hidden blade within the smile?
It is precisely when dwelling in leisure that one may discuss the maladies of Chan; jade and stone must rely on a skilled craftsman to be distinguished.
Next, Mimi Xin of Nengren Monastery at Mount Yan sent me a verse on the theme of "Holding Beyond the Category.
Who else could it be? Who among those who should know me? Since the departure of Longfeng, there have been no venerable elders;
now, in the Yan Dang mountains, there comes a great master. To raise a child, one does not employ the art of picking leaves; to benefit others, one must pull out the nails.

Rooted in doubt, I too wish to follow you with my short staff. Amidst ten thousand layers of mountains and ten thousand branches of water, I mourn Master Tianjing as he departs alone from Qiantang, bound by circumstances.
For five hundred days and nights, we shared a guest-window; let not the cold waters detain the wild geese.

The shadow turns as the gale suddenly fells the creeping vines and the stumps; the golden coffin reveals the assembly with its twin lotus feet exposed. Upon whose shoulders alone shall the cauldron of the lineage be carried?
Gazing west toward Vulture Peak, I am moved by deep emotion; of one such as you, the lion’s roar has become peerless.
I present this to the Venerable Shangren for his examination of the Lotus Sūtra and his request for a *du-jiè* (ordination certificate):
seven scrolls of numinous texts, one phrase that penetrates all. It does not hinder the manifestation of the True Doctrine wherever one may be.

While the "City of Transformation" is certainly fit for lodging, how could the "Jewel Place" tolerate lingering traces for long? When the Fragrant Elephant crosses the river, he must do so to the very bottom; lest he be struck by the lash of the "Not-Light" [Bodhisattva].
Exerting effort, this practice will surely achieve what is rare to encounter. May the dew of grace descend in profusion from the Nine Palaces.

As the venerable Master Jiu was sent to test his mastery of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṃitā Sūtra* and requested a certificate of ordination, he picked up the "Vajra-eye" atop his crown. From then on, his daily conduct and hidden reserves were no longer ordinary; the four marks have been fundamentally non-abiding.

Attached! How could the Three Minds possibly have a continuous transmission? Seeking outside of words and speech, one supports heterodox doctrines; seeking within sounds and forms, one obscures the True Source.
Cast aside the idle prediction of Dīpaṃkara; the precious seal in the void has layered brocade patterns.
As the venerable monk departs for the examination on the Heart Sūtra and requests his ordination certificate, the Prajñā has no need for cultivation;
its power of wisdom is replete. The original essence of sentient beings and Buddhas is identical. How could its radiance be obstructed by the sense organs and their objects?
Let it pass through freely, even if ensnared by the aggregate of consciousness. When Kumārajīva translated it, it flashed like lightning; where Avalokiteśvara practices, he captures [the thief].
Pure breeze. You should study diligently with the venerable masters of the Central Kingdom. I beg for their subtle words to dispel my ignorance.
I see Master Zuan off as he attempts to obtain a *du-chie* (ordination certificate) through the *Yuanjue Jing*;
the Great Luminous Treasury is free from all entanglements. Face-to-face encounters are as numerous as hemp seeds; once the four ailments are suddenly removed, gold is revealed.
The ore has just been refined; the jade reveals its flaws. Illusion arises and illusion perishes; the bubble returns to the water. Fully releasing and fully gathering, the guest arrives home.
Having received the numinous talisman, it hangs from the elbow; to settle the mind, there is no need to seek elsewhere.

The Venerable Shiwu’s patched robe is draped high; Zuilu, who could recognize that I am not my former self? Xinghua was indeed able to carry out the true command; Kebin truly did not fall into deviant paths. Before the hall, clouds of fragrant rice steam gather;

the golden mallet within the sleeve—[is it for striking? *Note: The final character "膽" (dǎn) appears to be a scribal error or fragment; in the context of Chan literature, this line typically concludes with a reference to the golden mallet used for striking, often implying a decisive or transformative action.*
The vital energy is coarse; with a single blow, empty space is reduced to dust. Casually, he raises up the old barbarian.

To the attendant Lin, I show that the tracks of the Fragrant Forest are still worth following. These fine words are secretly inscribed upon the paper robe; warm and solid, they always contain the stone.
The jade light shines indistinctly like a bead rolling on a platter; it is pushed away, yet flickering flames arise from within the waves.
Startled, pairs of fish leap from the treetops; sometimes they vie for victory, sometimes they contend for inferiority. Zhaozhou was originally but a single donkey.

In commemoration of Master Zongji, fifty-five years since his birth: his resolve was dedicated solely to investigating the teachings and he also mastered Chan. In his contemplation of the mind, he often lamented his own dullness and ignorance;

through the practice of counting the breaths, he hoped deeply to diminish his sleep. Even while suffering from illness, he constantly recited the jade-like verses with his own lips; at the moment of death, his eyes alone beheld [the truth].
The Golden Immortal, reflecting on the story of planting pines with white hair, could not help but feel a sense of melancholy in his solitary heart.

He showed that Zhiyuan’s pursuit of the Way without a teacher was a waste of effort; to act excessively is to bring shame upon the ancestral tradition. Being unable to resolve one's thoughts, one must simply focus exclusively [on the practice].
Silence. First, you must harbor doubt, fearing you might fall into emptiness. When raising the *huatou*, you must be earnest and persistent.
Do not chatter with others; do not be hasty. This old monk does not speak at leisure; I wish to force the living snake to transform into a dragon.
A Seven-Character Quatrain to Show Chan Practitioner Yun:
The Three Phrases of Yunmen offer no pointing-out; The Five Ranks of Dongshan are beyond contrivance. When a patch-robed monk steps upon them, he cannot step upon them.
He puts on his worn-out straw sandals from the twelve streets and laments that Master Dayuan of Daimai has already entered the cycle of rebirth;
as the sun sets, he grieves in vain over a heap of ashes— now one knows where he will become a donkey for some household.
The horse sheds its coat and comes again. In the same rhyme, I inscribe this for Gaozhai (The High Studio):
The High Studio is silent and still, overlooking a clear pool; Fragrance rises from the earthen cauldron throughout the twelve hours. At dawn, one returns to meditation beneath the pines.
Upon the stone, where traces of moss spread green, a *kāṣāya* robe is laid out.
This gift for the hat-makers and others is a single head-covering; its corners are tied and its woven texture is entirely free. Whether saint or commoner, all are covered by it.
Set it aside! When Yang is raised up, who can offer the price?
At Yu'an, the secluded thatched gate stands open all day long; most travelers turn back halfway. Zhaozhou’s feet tread upon the four heavens.
Below. For a thousand ages, he has been outdone by those who have fallen into his trap.
In response to Shao’s inquiry while ill:
having gained entry, the body is at last secure. Selling not an inch of land, he establishes the family tradition. By the stream, the stone woman first conceives.
Pregnant. Two strands of hair hang down among the grasses and trees.
Following the original rhyme, I respond to Netci’s Mōngtáng and Ānxītáng:

All worldly conditions have been shed like snow melting in a cauldron; the three realms are empty as wind sweeps away the smoke. At the gate, the wheels and hooves of travelers are as numerous as those at a great furnace.

Boiling over. Wearing short clothes that rustle as he sits in deep meditation, Master Daoshian (who passed away leaning on his desk with his fist clenched against his forehead) has yellow arsenic in his mouth and sinews in his eyes;
the slightest touch provokes his anger. His fist serves as a pillow, yet it remains high.
Lying down, there is no longer anyone to block my chest or drive me away.
Amidst the sound of pines at Master Zhongbin’s eaves roaring like a raging tide, my dream-soul has drifted several times upon a fishing skiff. The golden hook does not seek out tiny scales.
Ascending directly into the vast blue ocean to fish for the six giant tortoises, he entrusted himself to Master Jianxin of Dingshui.
At Dingshui, there are no waves lashing against the heavens; the source flows from the Putong era. Dragon eyes and hawk eyes are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Gradually, he managed to pierce the nostrils of that fellow.

He sent [this] to the Venerable Master Linggu of Qingliang, who rides astride a golden-maned lion cub and displays his full majesty atop the summit of Mount Wutai; Mañjuśrī makes a clamor that resounds through the heavens.
The Ground: Not manifesting great compassion before the opportune moment, he sends this "mashed yellow tuber" from Miaoyuan Shouzuo to cure hunger.
With a heart like a wall and eyes like eyebrows—seek out the meaning after Zhaozhou has departed.
A few words: there is a fist held up toward whom?
Paying respects at the stupa of Master Qiujiang, who was buried alive for twenty years at Songyan—his eyes and nostrils remain as they were. I have come wishing to rouse the nāga.
In the flash of a flint, the separate transmission is spoken. To the cotton-worker Jiang Sheng, he showed the flower-splitting at Dangyang;
let you watch it unfold. Long or short, let go or pull back as the moment requires; turning over the face-skin, strike lightly.
Folded. Clearly, not even a single hair-tip is revealed.
Ten Verses on Miscellaneous Sayings from Pine Cliffs:
Having divined a mountain dwelling to sever ties with neighbors, I find peace in the state of poverty and remain at peace therein. A single threadbare robe, layer upon layer...
Supplement: Lift it up and see how many catties it weighs!
Beyond the Stone Gate Barrier, the celestial ladder is perilous; yet if one can cast away body and mind, it is not difficult to reach. To inform you, travelers from the five lakes:
come well to this place and climb together.

Since ancient times, tigers and leopards have been many in the deep mountains; if you attempt to subdue them with a contrived mind, they immediately become demons. The seeds of great compassion know the intentions of people;
by day, they lead their cubs past the front of the hermitage.

In every thought-moment, non-arising, one naturally enters the subtle; The rice in the jar is exhausted, yet the belly remains hungry. Deep in the night, beneath the moon, the knocking at the door is urgent;
The practitioner from Jiaoxi returns with his alms-bowl.
Grasses, trees, smoke, and mists proclaim the orthodox command; what need has this poor monk for such earnest exhortation? Leaning alone upon the balustrade, there is nothing to be said;
upon the surface of the pond, the minnows gather their heads to listen.

Sitting cross-legged in silence, count the breaths within the nostrils; at first they are short, but you must know that over time they naturally lengthen. At evening, descend from the seat and walk once around;
in the stone incense burner, how many sticks of incense have been burned away?

The mind has nothing that can be realized, so why seek realization? The Way is fundamentally unaccomplished; how could it be accomplished? My wild nature delights in being a companion to springs and rocks;
my reclusion is not for the sake of fleeing fame.

When the mind is at ease, only then is there true leisure; only when the mind is at ease can one speak of dwelling in the mountains. Within the mountains, there is more than enough for a life of leisure;
yet when the mind is not at ease, dwelling there becomes even more difficult.
Ten days in the mountains, nine of which have been rain; green fruit falls incessantly from the treetops. A white dog follows its tracks into the grass;
startled, a bamboo pheasant flies up into the tree.

On an overcast autumn morning, flashes of lightning streak across the sky. I rise to wash my earthenware pot and cook a porridge of *kodo* millet. Gently probing the embers in the hearth, I find no fire remaining;
from the neighboring temple, the sparse tolling of bells drifts over the distant ridges.
The Librarian Jian braved the military campaigns to visit me at Anyan while seeking refuge; he presented me with two verses:
"Ciming changed his clothes to see Fenyang; He did not shrink from the arduous length of the road.
Considering that I am old and lack any skill, Your coming from afar—surely there is something left unexamined?"
Distinct features meet as eyes resemble eyebrows; at the parting of ways, there is no need for further prodding or piercing.
Firmly grasp the staff held in hand; this is the foremost branch of the Eastern Land.
Entrusting this Dharma to my nephew Yan Sidao:
having eliminated the two wonders of Jianyuan, the five-colored phoenixes shall finally spread their wings in the azure sky.
The achievements of Tengzhou are not difficult to carry on, all the more so since the universe within your breast is vast.
Show Zhong, the Abbot:
let go from emptiness so that not a single thing remains; yet do not see the person who lets go from emptiness.
If you say there is someone who can let go, I guarantee you have not yet penetrated the golden dust.

The Dharma-nephew Xuan Da-yu demonstrates the teaching by using the Dharma to teach the Dharma—there is no separate Dharma; he transmits mind through mind—there is no different mind. Wondrous Virtue and Śāriputra never met from the beginning;
the black cat and the white ox are the true intimates.
In presenting this to Attendant Heng, I constantly recall Attendant Shan of the Golden Phoenix Hall; his manual skill and functional mastery were wondrous and inexhaustible.
In a casual moment he produced a mere piece of stone, leaving even Cuiyan Zhen Dianxiong utterly bewildered.
In the same rhyme, I send this to Zu’ān at Mount Dàméi:
Reading the scriptures by day and reading the scriptures by night, The radiance of his eyes rivals the brightness of the moon. At times he accepts no offerings from the devas;
When hungry, he eats pine blossoms, his very bones pure.
Paper Curtain, following the rhyme of Venerable Ren’an:
From now on, I need not fear the fierce winds blowing; A single sheet of cold clouds hangs down on all four sides. Fortunate that it is already luminous and pure white;
Do not come within its precincts to scatter pearls.
Xiu’an’s hermitage serves as a site for the Way;
Master Zhufang is like wood gnawed by the wind and decayed by the rain—hollow and utterly simple. Not even half an inch of its beams and rafters remains solid.
Were it not for one who is willing to sacrifice body and risk life, how would they dare to come inside this house and lay their head down to sleep?
As I see the white rice of Qing-shui in Jiang-xi being sent off by Master Zhu,
every grain picked up is a true pearl; one knows not where chaff and husks might be found,
yet he seeks a horse-winnowing basket from Jiang-xi once more.
To the attendant Cuiyan Yi, I gave a summer of eastern talk and western talk. Zhiyi recorded it with great clarity: "The old master Cuiyan entered the mud and entered the water;
his eyebrows fell out entirely and will not grow back again."
Entrusted to Master Benchu at Fulong, a stone chime is struck at dawn after the rain; its resonance therein is most clear and full.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions there is no path to travel, yet now someone comes to continue the orthodox transmission.
To Lang Xingtian:
You have personally verified the truth and harbor no doubt; it is like jade within a stone awaiting someone to point it out, or like gold leaping from the furnace.
All empty pretenses and clever tricks have been worn away; nothing surpasses this single, authentic heart.
Inscription on the Painting of Huating Chuanzi Receiving Jiashan:
He capsized the boat and departed; already both sides were smeared with mud. Today, master and disciple part ways; without a word, we gaze at the painting.
Sending off Master Xing: "Mind is Buddha" is a tiger leaping from a cliff;
"Neither mind nor Buddha" is a bird caught in a net. Do not casually unfold this within the cooking pot;
beneath the knees of a true man lies gold.
Inscribed for Layman Wuxiang (by the Song Scholar):
His words do not touch upon the subtle distinctions of "leaving" or "non-leaving"; He brushes past Yunmen’s “Look at the mirror! and “Aha!
Extending the hand that wields the brush in the Jade Hall, He turns his broom upside down to paint the brows of a beauty.
Seeing Master Yan off on his journey to Jinling to practice Chan:
I fear only that he may lose his way; for it is not a matter of establishing a home, but rather of breaking one down.
If he should meet with the Scholar Song of Jinhua, tell him that even the iron tree will bloom.
At the dwelling place of Elder Cuisanshing, the path of the teaching must be made to cease; when speaking, do not allow the faculty of thought to arise.
The Tathāgata’s great jewel-flower king-throne is not comparable to an ordinary blackwood platform.

When he showed the prostration at Potalaka, [the Master] said, "In the monk’s quarters there is Avalokiteśvara; you have been vexed by Avalokiteśvara. He then exclaimed, "Alas! O Great Man! How could it be better than being free from affairs?
This was shown to the Venerable Qi, the Rector.
In the monastic groves, legal battles are an everyday occurrence; having been struck with the staff, how can one also be fined?
Although Xinghua was able to carry out the correct command, the practical advantage fell to Kebin.
Preface for the Venerable Vinaya Master Youfang:
In his day, when Linji visited Huangbo, there was Muzhou lurking behind him; today, fortunately, such a person is absent, so you may enjoy displaying your elegance wherever you go.
To show wisdom and awaken the mind:
when traveling on pilgrimage, one must carry one's eyes; when putting on clothes and eating food, one must know the proper time. A hundred-year lifespan is but the snap of a finger;
to apply oneself with diligence even now would be too late.

I show you, my disciple and grandson, this far-reaching plan and these words of truth; you must believe and accept them. This great matter of leaving the household life is no small cause. Do not act like a blind donkey following a large herd.
The robe and bowl of the Patriarchs require someone to transmit them.
Postscript on the Verse for the Title "Zhuxian":
When I first composed the verse titled "The Epithet of Zhuxian," some remarked that it was a gift-gatha rather than a verse for an epithet. Throughout my life, I have been fond of...
Hearing of my errors, I have amended them without parsimony; thus, I have once again composed this "Eulogy for Zhuxian.

Now, that which we of our school call a "eulogy" (song) should borrow concrete events to manifest ultimate principle, awakening the mind-ground so that phenomena and principle are blended and unified, pure and without admixture—like the flavor of clarified butter or the fragrance of the *campaka* flower, such that upon the slightest sensory contact of the nose or tongue, one falls directly into non-attainment (*aprāpti*).
The mind flows through the four limbs with a refreshing clarity; how could this be merely like the secular books that only describe the outward manifestations of magnificent virtue?

During the Chunxun era of the late Song dynasty, whenever various venerable masters composed verses for parting, for expressing their inspiration, or for praising the significance of their dharma names, they all employed the *song* (eulogy) form, taking four lines as the standard.
Their compositions were of the utmost refinement; even if one were to erase them...
The titles are given, yet their meanings are self-evident. It is like a poem written on an examination topic (*shengti shi*):

unless one has realized the profound and subtle through personal verification, mastered the ancient classics through broad study, and thus encounters the source at every turn or finds the correct path at every step, it is impossible to rely upon these titles to chant forth and express the profound essence.
Those who attempt this later have neither known the fundamental source nor possess sufficient talent and learning; they merely...

They strive for grandiosity and vigor, seeking to correct the habits of the Xuanchun era through blunt directness. Yet, some grasp the principle while neglecting the facts, others grasp the facts while neglecting the principle;
there are even those who lose both fact and principle altogether. Failing to examine their own failings, they instead lightly criticize the magnificent works of their predecessors.
Upon seeing them, they immediately raise their brows and gape with their mouths, assuming an air of contempt as if they were defiling something sacred. Occasionally...

Whenever one encounters those of this age who transcend conventional measures and speak in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*), they look upon such teachings with bewildered incomprehension and inevitably dismiss them as erroneous.
Yet, when they wish to cite evidence to deceive and mislead beginners, they further claim:

"That which was composed during the Xianchun era was like that, whereas what is being done now is the opposite. Alas, how extreme is their perversity and confusion! I have always found this deeply unsatisfying.
Within this context, as I have here once again composed verses in the *zhuxian* style, I have ventured to add these further remarks of mine and recorded them in full below.
May those who understand not deride me for this.
On the Snowy Cliff atop Mount Bako, I write:

Since the beginning of our school, at the moment of transmission from master to disciple, it has been like a swift thunderclap shattering a mountain or a frost-bitten bow splitting an arrow—how could there be any room for deliberation?
When Gao Feng first met Xueyan at the North Creek Pagoda, as soon as he offered his greetings, [Xueyan] struck him. Not...

This prevented his upward-reaching claws and fangs from being revealed. Furthermore, during the Tianning encounter, when a question and answer reached a point where no further logic could be extended, it was precisely the moment to sever his life-root completely, making him a free and unencumbered man.
At that time, you ought not have let him go; instead, you provided him with a spreading tangle of complications, causing him to remain stuck in the "dead gate" (sīgān) without finding a way out.
This was at that time. Now, observing this book, which recounts gains and losses in detail and addresses them to his teacher, one sees there are matters that simply cannot be left unaddressed;
how could they be measured by ordinary sentiments or shallow understanding? I have heard that when Xueyan was residing at Yangshan, he happened to arrive in Hangzhou and stayed at Lingyin Monastery;
he specifically dispatched a monk to Mount Tianmu to invite [Zhaozhou] to meet him.
I fear that this was triggered by this letter. Yet Gaofeng had already established his "death barrier" and would no longer leave the mountain.
When the monk returned with the message, Xueyan remarked, "A fellow who carries a roof-beam.

I say that had Gaofeng heard the summons and suddenly decided to leave the mountain to meet him, he would surely have suffered the calamity of deafness for three days; he was already firmly ensnared by Xueyan’s stratagem.
There is nothing to bestow. He is merely a fellow carrying a wooden plank on his shoulder; he is like a medicinal bag behind a funeral carriage. Nevertheless, tell me:
does this remark by Xueyan signify that he accepts him or not? Is there a transmission or not? Try to discern and distinguish it.
Inscription on the True Portrait of Master Dahui, the Ancestor of Miaoxi.
During the Southern Song period, his monastic lineage was as steep and formidable as that of Deshan and Linji;
his wisdom and eloquence were as vast and expansive as those of Nanyang Huiyuan. At that time, many virtuous scholars and officials were devoted to this Way.
There are none who do not wish to enter his gate and receive his exhortations; how much more so for those of us who wear the saffron robes!

He often said to his students: "In my place, we speak the 'clam and oyster Chan. As soon as one opens their mouth, they see nothing but common treasures; yet when I speak, it is of rare and wondrous jewels.

This is because my realization is stable and solid, and my teaching is precise and correct. It is like wind blowing across water, naturally forming ripples; how could it involve the calculations of emotional consciousness?"
If you compare them by means of written words and language, [you will see that] being sharp, novel, and meticulous is used for self-glorification.
If you say my words are not to be trusted, please examine this letter.
Postscript to the Reprint of the *Ten Precepts Treatise* (*Shiguilun*).
The *Ten Precepts Treatise* was composed by Chan Master Fayan, the tenth-generation descendant of Caoxi.

After the Master personally met Dizang and received his instructions, every opening of his mouth and movement of his tongue was nothing other than resolving the entanglements and removing the fetters for others.
For instance, when a monk asked, "What is one drop of water from the Cao source? the answer was, "It is one drop of water from the Cao source.
Furthermore, when the monk Huichao asked, "What is the Buddha? the answer was, "You are Huichao.

To provide such instructions is like trying to cook rice from iron nails or boiling soup from wooden shavings; it is an attempt to satisfy the hunger of all people in the world, yet it truly leaves them...
Since there is no place for lower teeth [to bite], how could one possibly wish to bind others with the phrasing and meanings of literary compositions?
The composition of this treatise was intended merely as a remedy for the disease of stifled and muffled doctrinal proclamations of the time; it was undertaken out of necessity.

Some may say that because the Master’s realization was stable and secret, and his insight was vast and profound, he therefore resorted to this work to cast aside his own literary brilliance and eloquence.
The commentator is mistaken. In the year Wuyin (1234), the library keeper Yue of Nanping produced this text and once commissioned me to transcribe it.
It was carved onto printing blocks at the Jizhao Pagoda Temple on Mount Jing. When Mount Jing suffered from the ravages of war and fire, the blocks were likewise consumed by the flames.

Now, the venerable Master Min of Wei-yu on Mount Tai has donated his own funds to re-carve this edition of the old manuscript previously transcribed by me, and has requested that I write a preface for it.
I have carefully examined the worn-out paintings of former days;

they are truly like those who, in the past, beheld the image within the jar at Xia-kou or the inscription upon the beam at Lang-ya—truly matters belonging to a different age. Alas! From this day forward...
If those who read this treatise can truly examine their own ailments and the state of their minds as Zen masters do, and are willing to take its excellent medicine,
would that not be most excellent?
Inscribed upon the small-character *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* by the Venerable Gao.
The Zen practitioner Tiantai Jing showed me a small-character copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written by the late Gao Shangren.
