Its length was no more than three inches plus a fraction, and its width was barely four inches. At first glance, it resembled a swarm of ants gathered over a piece of meat.
It shimmered and vibrated; one could not discern its beginning or end. Upon entering meditative concentration and observing it with clarity, I traced its layout and examined its characters.
Every single character was distinct and vivid, without even a half-stroke of error.

When I imagined the moment his fingers moved and his brush stroked, he attained great mastery—it was more than just writing in large, grid-marked characters. This is because I have often discussed the essence of the human mind.
Exquisite! It transcends all limits; it certainly cannot be discussed in terms of large or small.
If one’s cultivation were not pure and unified, and if one lacked the seamless, circular integration [of mind], how could one possibly take the great as small or the small as great?
The power of your daily cultivation and its seamless integration are evident here, Master. Some may say that Zhuangzi spoke of carving a monkey from the tip of a thorn, or of the hall...
The carving of this wheel below should be compared with this sutra; thus, it is certainly correct. However, I fear that the Master of the Bamboo City (Shi Zhi) will not be willing to add a word.
[This is] written after the words of Master Yuan of Fushan by Wuzhun.

In the past, whenever scholars sought admonitions from the Elder Chiwu of Yushan, he would often take out paper and ink to draw a grid like a measuring cup, within which he would write the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra* and the words of ancient worthies to respond to them; at the bottom of the paper, he would record only the date.
He merely inscribed his own name and did not add a single additional character. This was because he shared the same tongue as the Buddhas and Patriarchs and taught with the same intent;
the value lay in guiding people toward the point of entry, rather than in the mere display of calligraphic skill.

Furthermore, this accords with the spirit of the ancients who "transmitted but did not compose. Now, observing the hand-written manuscript of the late Master Zhengxu, it records the words of Master Yuan.
One letter. Since there is no signature or seal to examine, it remains entirely unknown who composed it; one can only suspect that this was because of reading its words.

Suddenly, a surge of inspiration stirred within me, and I could not help but express it through brush and paper to show to students. This, too, accords with the spirit of Yushan, who recounted the teachings of others rather than composing his own.
When one examines Cao Yuan’s *Zhengxu* (Continuation of the Correct) and sees how he encountered Pō’ān, one realizes that these two were like brothers within the Dharma;
whatever they practiced and enacted must have been the result of diligent study and discussion—how could it have been anything but so?
The Sixth (and Final) Volume of the Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Shunzhong.
Respectfully written by the Dharma-nephew Bhikṣu Wénwěi, Abbot of Puzhao Chan Monastery in Zhènjiāng Prefecture.
The Record of the Venerable Monk Yun of the Empty Chamber at Tiantai:

How great indeed is the Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs! Transmitted from mind to mind, it reached Master Dajian of the Tang dynasty, whose branches and lineages spread through the Five Dynasties and flourished during the Song.
It declined during the Yuan, when the monk Chongli served as an imperial preceptor.
These masters’ monasteries stand in view of one another, and the sounds of their bells and drums never cease; how could this be insignificant?

Generally, students see only those whose rank is high and reputation exalted, who stir the hearts of those far and near, and thus they come toward them like moths to the wind, eager to receive the Dharma without leisure, yet unaware that those who have attained the true flavor of Caoxi are perhaps few. This cannot but be considered a mark of having some discernment.
This is why he sighed so deeply. Chan Master Wumen of Tiantai resided within a monastic community and was invariably careful in choosing his teachers.

Indeed, through the Eye of the True Dharma (*saddharmadṛṣṭi*), he surpassed the ranks of the patriarchs and gathered up their legacy from over a millennium ago to enlighten those who were blind and deaf.
Was this not a feat that transcended the world? The Master’s name was Wumen; his courtesy name was...
Shuzhong, also known by the pen-name Kongshi, was a native of Linhai in Tai province. His clan name was Chen; his father was named Shou and his mother was of the Lin family.

When he was seven years old, he entered the local school, where he could recite the texts he read without the need for repeated instruction. Before reaching the age of twenty, he informed his parents of his wish to become a śramaṇa.
He went to Mount Jing to rely upon Master Jizhao Duan, under whom he shaved his head and received the full precepts (*upasampadā*).
At Zhaoqing Lusi, the following year he visited Master Lingshi Zhi of Jingci. The year after that, he went to Fengshan Yangfen, where he met Master Liyuan.
Master Ling had received the transmission from Master Baoshou of Fangshan; his realization was profound and far-reaching.
The Master inquired into the Dharma-gates with great detail regarding both subtle and major matters. Subsequently, he returned to Mount Jing to pay his respects to Master Jizhao.
The Master was then assigned to reside in the Zhemu (Nest for Birds) Hall. At that time, Mount Jing served as a reservoir for monks from all quarters;
whenever the Master displayed his talents, his reputation grew daily. Later, he traveled east to Siming and visited Master Zhidi of Taibai, where he served as the keeper of the library for ten years.
Cai, together with Master Cong of Mukan and Master Xing of Dazong, went to Mount Zituo in Taizhou to visit Master Dao of Zhuyuan.
Because he had not yet resolved the koan regarding the dog having no Buddha-nature, he asked the Master; as soon as he opened his mouth, he was met with a shout.
The Master attained great enlightenment, such that sweat poured down from every pore of his body. He then presented a verse, saying: "The dog has no Buddha-nature. Spring..."
The color [of his robes] filled the imperial capital. Inside Dongyuan of Zhaozhou, a gourd hung upon the wall.
The Official burst out laughing and said, "Even if you understand it this way, how can you succeed? The Master shook his sleeves and departed.

Later, while conversing with his fellow practitioners Cong and Xing about matters of the "Ultimate," the Master said, "This matter is like a fish drinking water; its warmth or coldness is known by itself. It certainly does not reside in words."
Regarding these words and letters: had we not encountered this old monk, we would have been buried for a lifetime by mere intellectual understanding.
Gentlemen, even if you possess a thatched roof over your heads, you should never forget your origins. When the three men appeared in the world, they offered incense;
indeed, it was just as he had said. Over a year later, he returned to Tiantong, while Guding Ming took charge of Jingshan.
He dispatched his disciples to summon the Master back to Mengtang Hall to deliberate upon the profound essence of the Dharma, establishing it as a model for scholars;
consequently, those who came to seek instruction were numerous. After five or six years, due to the perils of war, he sailed by sea and returned to Siming.

By nature, he did not delight in entering the world of public office, residing at mountain monasteries only twice, in both cases retiring after barely three years had passed. Previously, while the former master Ming was at Lingyan, he once dreamed...
When Master Táng’è resided at Ruìlóng, the master [Fǎ]yì was the successor of Jìzhào. The master said, "My original vow lies elsewhere; it cannot be diverted.
Thereupon, Yīxiāng was brought forth by Māo Zǐtuó Dàogōng to receive the Dharma once more. Later, he presided over Ruìyán in Tái.
Upon arriving, he addressed the assembly from within his quarters, saying: "One sits securely in the family hall; why, then, does the master of the house not recognize himself?"
He overturns the great ocean and crushes Mount Sumeru. On level ground, why can he not lift his foot?
His eye-sight pierces through the four worlds; why do his own eyebrows fall away entirely? Why is it that those who have offered words before and after him mostly fail to accord with his intent?
Such was the steep and towering nature of his spiritual pivot (*ji-feng*). Only then did students follow him in admiration; eventually, he retired from affairs and entered the pines.
Seated alone upon a crag. The "Pine Crag" was the retreat of Master Chanjiang Zan; it lay atop ten thousand mountains, rarely visited by human footsteps.
When the Master arrived there, he dismissed all his attendants and sent a sealed letter to the community at the monastery.

When the assembly opened the seal, they found it contained his parting words from the hall before leaving the monastery. They all wept and pleaded with him to return to the monastery, but the Master resolutely refused and would not consent.
In the summer of the seventh year of the Hongwu era of the Great Ming dynasty today, the ruler of the country of Japan dispatched an envoy to present tribute.
He further submitted a petition requesting that the Master convert his nation, offering a crystal rosary and a stone inkstone from Mount Emei as ceremonial gifts for the Master’s reception.
The Emperor summoned the Master to the palace precincts. The Master declined on account of his old age and illness;
the Emperor took pity on him and did not send him away, instead allowing him to remain at Tianjie Monastery. There, the master monk Quanshi Le invited him to his private quarters.

At that time, Song Jingliao of Jinhua was serving in the Hanlin Academy; whenever he had a day off from official duties, he would invariably visit the Master to engage in long and profound conversations about the Way.
The eminent scholars of the court at that time all held him in profound reverence and admiration.

In the winter of that year, he received an imperial decree to return east. Having already composed a preface for his recorded sayings, Duke Song sent a poem to express his sentiments after their parting.
In the seventeenth year, his disciple Juding resided at Cui Mountain in Yinzhou and invited the Master there to live in retirement; seekers from all quarters came to pay their respects.
There was not a single day that passed without [such occurrences]. A monk from Dali, whose teeth were capped with gold, heard the Master’s reputation while in the capital.

He entered Mount Cui specifically to pay his respects, leading over fifty followers who prostrated themselves at the foot of the Master’s bed and each requested a verse before departing. One day, the Master suddenly fell slightly ill.

When monks came to inquire after his health, the Master spoke only of Chan with all his strength; even as he lay ill, he exhorted them to value the ancestral Way for themselves, never uttering a single word regarding [his own condition].
Regarding the signs of the world, he took up his brush and wrote a verse, saying: "Seventy-eight years; there is no dharma that can be spoken.
This final phrase—let the pillar speak! *Duh!* He sat upright and passed away. This was indeed the tenth day of the seventh month in the nineteenth year of the Hongwu era, the Bingyin year.
He was seventy-eight years of age and fifty-nine years since his ordination. His final testament stated: "When I die, let there be no worldly funeral rites."
It is appropriate that you discard [this practice] entirely and do not carry it out. Only after cremation, one should scatter the charred bones among the bamboo by the water to manifest impermanence.
Since my youth, Master Ding has been restless in his dwelling; even when he resided at Mount Zhu to receive our support, the affairs were so numerous that morning and evening attendance was lacking.
How could I dare persist in the command to scatter the bones? Therefore, I purchased the permanent property of Mount Cui.

In the mountains, on a certain plot of land at Tangxie Yuan, on the fifteenth day of the twelfth month of that year, he was enshrined with his remains in a burial mound, and a stone stupa was erected upon it.
By nature, the Master was pure, upright, and sincere; he always maintained himself with humility and restraint.
He pursued the Way as if he had not yet attained it, and cultivated virtue as if he were never sufficient. His heart was especially kind and forgiving; whenever he saw a student...
If there was even a measure of goodness or an inch of merit, he would immediately rejoice at seeing it and speak of it as if it were his own.

He was exceptionally earnest in encouraging, supporting, and praising others, hoping they would achieve some accomplishment that would benefit the Dharma-gate. If they committed a transgression that was not of great harm, he never once rebuked them with anger.
When he encountered those of brilliant spirit, fearing they might find blunt speech difficult to accept, he would instead cite their past words and deeds from former times to instruct them.
He acted in such a way that [the faults of others] were subtly eliminated and silently cautioned against; thus, the monastics from all quarters loved and revered him as a compassionate mother.

Yet, whenever he encountered matters within the Dharma that violated the teachings or betrayed righteousness, he would invariably confront and rebuke them without the slightest leniency. From his youth until old age, the Master never let go of his books;

there was no scripture, whether internal or external, that he did not master with comprehensive breadth. When he composed literary works, poems, or gāthās, they invariably reached the heights of excellence.
His ancient compositions were immediately transmitted and recited by others without end. When at leisure, he would sit upright in silence, speaking little.

Whenever monastics requested Dharma discourses or Zen verses, he would take up his brush and write with divine spontaneity, satisfying each person’s intent without wishing to cause them prolonged delay.
His personal conduct was exceedingly pure and frugal; when advancing, he took nothing at all from what he received, and when retiring, he returned everything as it was.
As for those he provided for, they were exhausted and he had nothing left to carry away. His reverence for his teacher and his treatment of his friends were exceptionally earnest.
When Master Jizhao was alive, he served him with the utmost care; he would stand in attendance until the second or third watch of the night, never daring to withdraw unless commanded to do so.

After the Master passed away, he braved the great cold to transcribe the *Yulu* (Recorded Sayings); though his hands became afflicted by illness, he paid it no heed. Furthermore, he sought out Huang...
Duke Wénxiàn inscribed his stupa. As for the case involving Rúgōng of Yī’ān, who was a fellow disciple and dharma-relative:

when Rúgōng was residing at Bǎofú Monastery, there was a temple monk who harbored a grudge against him. It happened that a young boy died in the wilds, and the monk bribed the boy’s father to frame Rúgōng. Rúgōng was subsequently arrested and imprisoned.
The Master (Zhìyuán) was about to petition the provincial commissioner on his behalf and also requested influential figures within the Dharma community to provide assistance.
Thereupon he was released. After Yichan entered nirvana, [the author] further compiled those accounts worthy of recording and sought renowned public figures to commemorate the events;
the rest are of this same nature. Although he enjoyed himself in seclusion through the Way, he observed that the Great Dharma was declining.
Talent has fallen into obscurity; I have always been deeply concerned by this, an anxiety manifested in both my words and countenance.

Among my writings throughout my life, there are *Two Assemblies of Discourse* in several volumes, *Verses and Hymns* in several volumes, a re-presentation of one hundred ancient cases from Xuedou’s *Niangu*, a continuation of one hundred and ten ancient cases with verses following Dahui’s and Zhushan’s precedents, *Miscellaneous Records from the Mountain Hermitage* in several volumes, and [the work on] Purity...

*Tu-shi* (Earthly Verses), one scroll. Generally, regarding the writings of those who study external paths, their drafts are never preserved; however, this author has long been most familiar with the Master’s renowned reputation.
On two occasions, he visited Mount Cui to request an audience, to observe his demeanor, to listen to his discourse, and to read his writings.

These were found to differ not in the slightest from the accounts of his practices and deeds recorded in the *Xingye-ji* (Record of His Deeds) kept at the mountain peak. Undaunted by my own meager talent, I have composed this.
The inscription reads:
"The swelling of the Yellow River eventually ebbs away; the flourishing of the Way eventually diminishes. Among the prosperity of the Buddhas, none was greater than that of the Yuan [era].
Yet the Way has now declined, and the Master sighs daily over this. He sought out hidden retreats and visited secluded places until he realized the truth within the purple bamboo."
Transcending heaven and earth, he caused the rivers and mountains to tremble; yet the mountains did not become higher, nor the rivers deeper—it was the Master who possessed such height and depth.
He cut across all time, past and present; from the waters of Caoxi, he drew forth their current again. That this flow remains unceasing is due to the Master’s enduring glory.
Composed by Wu Sidao, a man of Mount Ming, on the day after the full moon in the ninth month of the Wuchen year of the Hongwu era. A Parting Verse for the Elder Bi,
Mind-Fountain (Xinquan), as he departs to pay his respects to Master Empty Chamber (Kongshi).
The foremost requirement for practicing Zen is to know the source. Throughout the four seas, only Old Shuzhong is heard of. Amidst the bright sun and blue sky, a thunderclap resounds;
all you fox-demons and malevolent spirits vanish into hiding.
Jinhua, Song Lian, pays his respects twice.
[End of] the Record of the Deeds of Chan Master Kongshi Yun of Tiantai.
